articles.title: How Milwaukee’s silly sausages became one of the most beloved spectacles in baseball
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers are deadly serious about their baseball this season.
articles.body: The Milwaukee Brewers are deadly serious about their baseball this season. Finishing with the best record in MLB, they’re hoping that this will be the year they can finally win a World Series after clinching a spot in the Fall Classic on Thursday. But this is a franchise that doesn’t always take itself too seriously, and the bright lights of October will help showcase one of the most wonderfully ridiculous servings in sport: The slapstick sixth-inning sausage race. It’s exactly as absurd as it sounds. Human runners, wearing 7-foot-tall foam costumes with goofy faces and colorful features depicting a Bratwurst, Polish, Italian, Hot Dog and Chorizo, race each other around home plate on the warning track. The comedically top-heavy sausages, which can easily topple forwards into the dirt, temporarily take center stage as the baseball players gaze on in amusement from their dugouts, sometimes wagering on the outcome. But from the very first race in the summer of 1993, these sausages have sizzled and arguably helped to modernize the most traditional American pastime. “I think the things that become iconic and popular are things that the fans adopt, as opposed to something forced on them,” Brewers’ President of Business Operations Rick Schlesinger explained to CNN Sports. “This was a perfect example of something innocent, a little silly, whimsical, but, you know, quintessentially Wisconsin.” Dating back to the 1800s, the state of Wisconsin was a popular destination for European immigrants, and they brought their love of meat and beer with them. The town of Sheboygan, just 60 miles north of Milwaukee, claims to be the “Bratwurst Capital of the World.” When the baseball team came along in 1969, the Brewers’ name indicated that they’d be leaning into their community’s roots. A quarter of a century later, local graphic designer Michael Dillon pitched the idea of a live-action sausage race to the team’s then-Vice President of Operations Gabe Paul Junior, but he says the notion of it seemed so obvious that everyone was probably thinking it. The team had already animated a cartoon film of three anthropomorphic sausages running across the Milwaukee skyline on the big screen and when they were seen to arrive at the gates of the stadium, the characters would race across the scoreboard as digital dots. Paul initially dismissed the suggestion – “I don’t think that’s going to fly,” Dillon recalled of their conversation – but he subsequently changed his mind. The Brewers wanted a special event to mark the return of the Brewers’ legend Paul Molitor, who had recently moved to Toronto, and a sausage race was it. Dillon said he quickly made the giant costumes out of foam rubber, contact cement and spray paint, and turned up to race in them on June 27, 1993. “When we put them on, we couldn’t stand up inside County Stadium,” he told CNN Sports, “We had to walk bent over with people holding them in front of us. When it came time for the sausage race, the gates opened up, we ran out and you cannot imagine what happened.” He says the roar of the crowd was deafening: “I mean, I was inside a tube of foam rubber, but I could hear this enormous sound.” In honor of his German grandfather, Dillon wore the “Brett,” the bratwurst costume with his green lederhosen. His business partner of Italian descent Dan Necci took “Guido,” the Italian chef, and his employee Jeff Paul, Gabe’s son, took the Polish sausage, “Stosh,” in his striped rugby jersey. Visibility inside the sausages was limited. “Oh my god,” Dillion exclaimed, “the hole to look out of was maybe, like, eight inches, and when you ran it bounced up and down, you couldn’t see where you were going, I ran into one of the other sausages.” Dillon said that because of the need for secrecy, they had only practiced running in the costumes once before the big day, they weren’t really prepared for the physical and navigational challenges. “Anyway, we ran across the field, I won, and the home plate umpire was pissed about it. He said that it was making the sport into a joke,” Dillon added. Dillon returned to his design studio with the costumes, wondering what would come next. A few weeks later, the Brewers called to say they wanted another race and when it started becoming a more regular event, he donated the costumes to the team and let them get on with it themselves. Knowing now what the race would later become, he told CNN, “My friends hound me that I should be getting money, but no, it’s fine. I had fun doing it and it has enriched my life, and that’s enough for me.” A couple of years later, the Brewers added a fourth link, “Frankie Furter,” a hot dog in a baseball uniform, and by the end of the 2000 season, when the team was preparing to move to a new stadium across the road, the video animation was dropped and the sausages began racing during every home game. In 2006, on the team’s first ever Cerveceros Day to celebrate Latin heritage and culture within baseball, “Cinco” the Chorizo made his debut in a sombrero. However, the spicy sausage wasn’t permitted to race full-time until 2007, because MLB prohibits the introduction new mascots during a season. Even in the bizarro world of meat racing, there are still rules to abide by. Over 30 years later, the event has transcended the Brewers, parodied and imitated in equal measure. More than half the teams in the league have their own versions of the mascot race – for example salmon in Seattle or presidents in Washington, D.C. – and Milwaukee’s famous five have been featured twice in commercials for ESPN’s SportsCenter show. In one, the sausages spoofed Pamplona’s Running of the Bulls, chasing panicked employees through a narrow office corridor. The Brewers prefer not to say who runs in the costumes, saying mostly they are franchise employees, members of the “Brew Crew,” but they admit that several players have competed and people with connections might be allowed in, too. In 2011, the Brewers’ then-first baseman Prince Fielder told the New York Times, “My wife’s done it. My two boys have done it. My wife’s cousin came and actually tore her A.C.L doing it. She took it like a champ.” The Brewers have embraced the sausages to the point that the race results are tallied along with their gameday reports, but the sausages have also been the subject of police reports and made national news. In 2013, the $5,000 Italian costume, went missing for two weeks until it surfaced at bar in Cedarburg. According to the bartender Jen Mohney, two men dropped the costume on the premises and told her, “You did not see anything.” She called the police as soon as they had left, telling the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel,“Like I didn’t just see two guys plop a sausage on a bar stool.” According to the 46-page police report, the officers responding to the call at TJ Ryans noted the tire tracks in the snow and evidence of a speedy getaway, plus a ziplocked bag with a note inside. “Sorry I’m such a sauced weenie,” it read. “You probably think I am the wurst. I started feeling the heat as the police began to ketchup by connecting the links. I know it was a greasy move so here I am.” Guido has been a magnet for controversy; a decade earlier he had been knocked to the ground when the Pirates’ first baseman Randall Simon took a swing at him with his bat from the visitor’s dugout, causing both the Italian sausage and hot dog to fall. Inside the costume, the 19-year-old University of Wisconsin student Mandy Wagner was laughing, and she still thought it was funny even when she learned of Simon’s involvement as she was being treated for a scraped knee at the first aid station. Nobody was laughing after the game, though, when Simon was arrested and booked for misdemeanor battery. Although he was never charged with a crime, Simon was suspended for three games, fined $2,000 by MLB and ordered to pay $432 by the sheriff’s department. Speaking about the incident to MLB.com in 2022, Wagner recalled the police visiting to take pictures of her injured pinkie and a “Good Morning America” news crew reporting live from her backyard. “They were criminalizing him,” she recalled, “and I didn’t feel like that was fair. I didn’t want to be a part of that.” Simon called to apologize and signed the notorious bat for her, she was also treated to a free vacation in his native Curacao. Headline writers had a field day, calling it “The Great Link Stink,” and so did the merchandise vendors who began selling T-shirts with the message ‘Don’t Whack our Wiener.’ Since the sausages began racing, the Brewers have only made it to the postseason eight times and their only World Series appearance came much earlier, in 1982. Now, there doesn’t appear to be any weak links, and both their players and their sausages could be ready for the heat of the biggest stage. Reflecting on the sausages’ enduring success, Michael Dillon says he still feels an emotional connection. “Oh, my babies,” he exclaims, whenever he sees them, and he always talks to the mascots at games. He didn’t see the original costumes again until he was commissioned to design the Miller Park logo, and they were under a pile of stuff. “Someone took them when they were being thrown away and they ended up being sold on eBay, which is where the new Wisconsin Cultural Historical Museum found them and purchased them,” he said, noting that the costumes will soon go on display. Interest in the sausages shows no sign of abating. Dillon also says that he’s going to be profiled by author Russell Florence in a book about 100 people who have changed the face of baseball, adding that he can see a direct link between the risible race and the highly successful sports and entertainment brand The Savanah Bananas. But he could never have imagined any of this back in the spring of 1993. “It’s just a fluke,” he explained. “They have personalities, they have nationalities,” everyone in the community feels as though they have a sausage to root for. Now retired from the McDill agency that he founded, Dillon says that he’s still invited back by the Brewers, and he’s thrown out the first pitch on the 20th and 30th anniversaries of the inaugural race. “Miller Brewing was my biggest client, we had some phenomenal jobs that were high profile, I published some travel books and got interviewed by the BBC, but that pales in comparison to this,” he said. “The one thing that everyone remembers me for is the racing sausages!” Note: This story was originally published in 2025 and has been updated.

articles.title: Watch Shohei Ohtani's Epic Reaction to Ending HR Drought on Video in Dodgers-Brewers NLCS Game 4
articles.summary: Shohei Ohtani broke out of his slump in a major way on Thursday night.
articles.body:
Shohei Ohtani broke out of his slump in a major way on Thursday night.

Ohtani was fired up after launching a three-run home run in the bottom of the second inning during Game 4 of the Los Angeles Dodgers' NLCS matchup with the Milwaukee Brewers.

It represented the four-time MVP's first homer since Aug. 18.

Ohtani was plagued by injuries during the regular season, as left knee inflammation forced the two-way star to stop pitching in July. The Dodgers later placed him on the 15-day injured list due to left knee and right biceps issues.

While Ohtani was able to join the team again before the end of the regular season, he struggled at the plate.

He posted a mere .558 OPS across five regular-season appearances upon returning and continued to fall below expectations once the playoffs started.

In seven postseason games heading into Thursday's action, Ohtani compiled a .182/.333/.182 slash line with seven strikeouts in 22 at-bats.

The Brewers lead the Dodgers 3-0 in the NLCS, but Los Angeles' chances of a comeback should improve if the 32-year-old can become a key contributor once again.

After all, Ohtani has recorded 139 home runs in his three years as a member of the Dodgers. He also racked up 11 homers in 33 postseason games during Los Angeles' playoff runs that ended with World Series titles in 2024 and 2025.

articles.title: Brewers sweep Dodgers to reach World Series for first time since 1982
articles.summary: Milwaukee will face either the Cleveland Guardians or the Tampa Bay Rays in the Fall Classic. The NLCS result ends Los Angeles’ bid to win three straight MLB championships.
articles.body: The Milwaukee Brewers are headed to the 2026 World Series after they swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series. The franchise, which has never won an MLB title, will be making its first appearance in the Fall Classic since 1982. Thursday’s result, a 6-4 Brewers victory in Game 4, ended the Dodgers’ hopes of earning dynasty status. Los Angeles entered the postseason as two-time defending champions, and a third straight title would have put it in rare air — the New York Yankees and the Oakland Athletics the only other teams to have accomplished such a feat. “We’re just happy for our fans and everybody that has been part of this organization and stuck with us over the years,” Brewers star Christian Yelich said on the Fox broadcast after the game. “We’ve been so close to this point so many times. To finally break through is a credit to our guys, our team. They stuck together and battled. We got down there early tonight, and we were like: ‘It’s going to be a great story when we win this. Stay together and start chipping away.’ And it’s exactly what they did.” The Dodgers jumped out to a 4-0 lead in the second inning Thursday. Kyle Tucker scored on an Andy Pages RBI single before superstar Shohei Ohtani hit a three-run home run 428 feet into the right-center field bleachers. But the Brewers would not go away. Jake Bauers hit a ground-rule double in the fourth inning, scoring William Contreras and Brice Turang to make it 4-2. In the fifth, David Hamilton singled to center, scoring Sal Frelick. Later in the inning, Dodgers reliever Alex Vesia walked in the tying run (credited to starter Tyler Glasnow for having initially loaded the bases). The Brewers took a 5-4 lead on Garrett Mitchell’s solo home run in the sixth inning and added an insurance run in the ninth on Hamilton’s bomb. “It’s absolutely surreal,” Mitchell said on the Fox broadcast after the game. “I don’t really got words. I’m just so proud of our team. To go down four [runs] really early, and you talk about the battle-tested Brewers, man. We got down early, and the belief in that dugout got stronger and stronger, and we fought our butts off and got back in here. It was incredible.” Milwaukee’s bullpen and timely hitting were key to the Brewers’ jumping to a 3-0 lead in the NLCS. In Game 1, star Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run over 4.1 innings but had incredible help once the Brewers’ bullpen came on. Four pitchers — DL Hall, Abner Uribe, Aaron Ashby and Trevor Megill — combined to give up two hits and no runs to preserve a 2-1 victory. Relievers once again helped Milwaukee in Game 2 after starter Logan Henderson struggled early. Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Uribe and Ashby combined to retire the last 15 Dodgers batters in order in a 7-4 win. In Game 3, rookie starter Robert Gasser went to Dodger Stadium and pitched five innings of scoreless baseball. Back-to-back home runs by Jake Bauers and Garrett Mitchell in the seventh inning gave the Brewers a lead they would not relinquish. The Brewers were the best team in baseball this season, leading MLB with 103 wins. Over 162 games, they had the best ERA in the National League (3.23) and have dropped that number to just 1.74 in the postseason. While Milwaukee does not boast the star power of the Dodgers, it has the National League Cy Young favorite in Misiorowski and a balanced lineup of hitters. Catcher William Contreras has been on fire in the playoffs, with three home runs, four walks and five RBIs while batting .370. Outfielder Jackson Chourio leads the team with seven home runs. The Dodgers “may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we got a bunch of gamers,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said after the win. “And the gamers won this week.” The Brewers will face the winner of the ALCS — the Cleveland Guardians lead the Tampa Bay Rays 2-1 in the series — in the World Series, which begins next Friday in Milwaukee.

articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers will get the chance to play for the franchise's first World Series title.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers will get the chance to play for the franchise's first World Series title.

The Brewers sealed an NLCS sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers with a 6-4 Game 4 win Thursday night in L.A.

The two-time defending World Series champions will head home while the Brewers advance to the championship series for the first time since 1982.

Yankees higher ups annoyed with Aaron Judge

Here's a look at the path ahead for the Brewers as the club prepares to face either the Cleveland Guardians or Tampa Bay Rays in the Fall Classic.

Game 4 @ CLE: Friday, Oct. 16 at 6 p.m. ET

Game 5 @ CLE: Saturday, Oct. 17 at 8 p.m. ET

Game 6 @ TB (if necessary): Monday, Oct. 19 at 5 p.m. ET

Game 7 @ TB (if necessary): Tuesday, Oct. 20 at 8 p.m. ET

Game 5 @ AL (if necessary): Wednesday, Oct. 28

Game 6 @ MIL (if necessary): Friday, Oct. 30

Game 7 @ MIL (if necessary): Saturday, Oct. 31

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts placed Shohei Ohtani back in the leadoff spot ahead of Game 4.

Ohtani, who has been playing through injuries, responded by hitting a three-run home run to give the Dodgers a 4-0 lead in the bottom of the second.

The Brewers chipped away at the early lead when Jake Bauers sent home two runs on a ground rule double in the fourth inning.

David Hamilton chased Dodgers starter Tyler Glasnow with an RBI single in the fifth.

Relief pitchers Evan Phillips and Alex Vesia were unable to stop the damage as the fifth inning continued. The Brewers loaded the bases before Bauers drew an RBI walk to even the score.

Garrett Mitchell opened the sixth inning with a 409-foot home run to give the Brewers their first lead of the game.

The Dodgers' Kyle Tucker made it to third base in the bottom of the sixth before JoJo Romero ended the frame by forcing Max Muncy into a swinging strikeout.

Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby got his team out of another jam by leaving Will Smith stranded on third in the bottom of the eighth.

Hamilton then padded the Brewers' lead with another solo home run in the top of the ninth.

Ashby retired his last three batters in order to close out the bottom of the ninth and clinch the NL pennant for the Brewers.

The Guardians pulled ahead in the ALCS with a 3-2 Thursday win over the Rays.

The Brewers will now wait for the result of the ALCS, which continues Friday with Game 4 in Cleveland, while preparing to open the World Series a week from Friday in Milwaukee.

articles.title: Dodgers 2026 Offseason Guide on Free Agents, Trade Targets, More Roster Shakeups After NLCS Sweep
articles.summary: After winning back-to-back World Series and feeling destined for a three-peat, the Los Angeles Dodgers ran into a Milwaukee Brewers-sized brick wall in the NLCS, swept by the same team they swept one year ago.
articles.body:
After winning back-to-back World Series and feeling destined for a three-peat, the Los Angeles Dodgers ran into a Milwaukee Brewers-sized brick wall in the NLCS, swept by the same team they swept one year ago.

Dynasties don't last forever, but is this one now kaput?

Or will the Dodgers be back with a vengeance in 2027?

Ahead, we'll take a look at Los Angeles' most noteworthy free agents and its best options for replacing them—whether internally, via free agency or via trade—before offering up a super early look at what the Dodgers' 26-man roster might look like on Opening Day.

There were 11 players who recorded at least 253 plate appearances for the Dodgers in 2026.

All 11 of those players are signed through at least 2027.

Needless to say, this offense is looking pretty darn good for next season, unless you're overly concerned about Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy and Mookie Betts starting to get up there in years.

However, Rojas is a pretty significant impending departure.

The versatile infielder appeared in at least 100 games in each of the past four seasons for the Dodgers, and even delivered that highly improbable home run in the ninth inning of Game 7 in the 2025 World Series.

Maybe they re-sign him for an age-38 campaign, but there are other options out there who could be the primary reserve at all four infield positions.

[Editor's Note: Rojas announced his retirement shortly after this was published.]

Replacing Hernández is less of a concern, as the Dodgers already grew accustomed to life without him. Due to injury, he appeared in just two of their first 108 games this season. And now they've got top prospect Josue De Paula ready to factor into the outfield rotation in a potentially big way in 2027.

By leaps and bounds, Skubal is Major League Baseball's most coveted free agent this winter. There's a decent chance he's going to break Yoshinobu Yamamoto's record-setting-for-a-pitcher $325M contract.

And, well, any time you're talking about a record-setting contract, you kind of have to assume the Dodgers are going to be part of that bidding war. For the time being, though, he's a free agent.

Among guys who have been Dodgers for more than three months, though, the biggest loss here would definitely be Vesia.

Over the past three seasons, Vesia has pitched in 207 games with a 2.45 ERA, including a team-high 72 relief appearances this season. He also entered this October with a 1.86 ERA in his 26 career postseason appearances, tallying two wins and four holds just last postseason.

Can they convince him to stick around? Or is Vesia headed for a nice big raise from a team that views him as a potential closer?

Phillips and Treinen both have even more closing experience than Vesia does, but both have been limited by injury over the past two seasons. Same goes for Graterol, who hasn't pitched in the majors since the 2024 World Series.

In Shohei Ohtani, the Dodgers have a four-time MVP at DH. They also have former MVPs at first base and shortstop in Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts. Both their catcher (Will Smith) and third baseman (Max Muncy) are three-time All-Stars. The outfield trio of Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages has combined for seven All-Star rosters.

And at second base...they have Tommy Edman.

He has been worth more than 20 bWAR in his career, but hasn't been able to stay healthy over the past three seasons. Meanwhile, the in-house backup plans of Alex Freeland and Hyeseong Kim haven't proven themselves worthy of everyday work.

If they're adding anything to this position player group this winter, it almost has to be someone capable of manning second.

We previously mentioned that Alex Vesia is a big loss, if he signs elsewhere in free agency. He led this team with 20 holds, while fellow free agents Evan Phillips and Blake Treinen combined for 14.

In Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott, they do still have quite the one-two punch at the back end of the bullpen. In an ideal world, Dave Roberts gets to play matchups with both his well-compensated lefty and his well-compensated righty racking up 20 holds and 20 saves.

But reinforcing that bridge from the starting rotation to the tandem of closers with more than 100 career saves is a near-must.

They didn't need Kyle Tucker or Edwin Díaz this past winter. Nor did they need Blake Snell the previous offseason.

However, the Dodgers' biggest signings rarely have anything to do with needs.

So when you hear about their efforts to re-sign Tarik Skubal—or to snag 3B/OF Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato whenever he gets officially posted—just know it's because they can; not because they feel they must.

Early MLB Offseason Predictions on Free Agency and Trades 🔮

When all of the Dodgers' big league regulars are healthy, it's going to be difficult to find regular opportunities for their top prospects who might otherwise be ready for The Show.

In Josue De Paula and Mike Sirota , though, Los Angeles has two of the top outfield prospects in all of baseball.

We got a sneak peek at De Paula in September while Shohei Ohtani was on the IL, and he did not disappoint even a little bit. In 42 trips to the plate, he went 10-for-31 with 11 walks and a home run. And in 124 games played at Double-A Tulsa, the 21-year-old triple-slashed .303/.401/.547 with 27 home runs and 31 stolen bases

Sirota didn't do quite that much slugging, but he sure does have a knack for reaching base. He had a .458 OBP in his 143 games played in college. And his OBP through 167 minor-league games? Also .458. How very Juan Soto-like of him.

The Dodgers also have James Tibbs III waiting in the wings. He hit 30 home runs this season at Triple-A Oklahoma City. But even as a 1B/LF/RF triple threat, he's at the mercy of Freddie Freeman, Teoscar Hernández and Kyle Tucker to create an opening.

And on the pitching front, watch out for RHP Christian Zazueta . He has only made 12 starts at Double-A thus far and is probably still at least a year away. But he has averaged 11.8 K/9 and 6.3 K/BB over the past two seasons and might be on the fast track to the majors.

2B Brandon Lowe OR 2B Jazz Chisholm Jr. OR 2B Luis Arraez OR 2B Gleyber Torres

In most years, the pool of second basemen available in free agency is...uninspiring.

After Gleyber Torres accepted his qualifying offer from Detroit last November, the 2B market pretty much became Luis Arraez or bust. And the year before that, Torres off a disappointing walk year and an injured Ha-Seong Kim were the best options out there by far.

But in addition to Torres and Arraez yet again, the Dodgers could fix their second base problem with either Brandon Lowe's 35 home runs or Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s combination of 19 home runs and 41 stolen bases.

We'll see which route they decide to go, but let's just say we're not expecting Alex Freeland to make 80 appearances at second base in 2027.

How do you simultaneously replace Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernández?

With two-time, soon to be named three-time utility Gold Glover Mauricio Dubón, of course.

After a season in which he started in 149 games for Atlanta, he's surely looking for a similar opportunity to play nearly every day, which wouldn't the case with the Dodgers. But maybe they can talk him into a situation where he starts 15-20 games at every position except for pitcher and catcher.

Whether the fact that they traded for him gives them any sort of leg up in this bidding war remains to be seen, but you have to know the Dodgers are going to make Skubal an offer they hope he can't refuse.

They do have Tyler Glasnow under team control through 2028, Yoshinobu Yamamoto through at least 2029, Blake Snell through 2030 and Shohei Ohtani through 2033, but Skubals don't exactly grow on trees.

If signing him means they have to subsequently trade away a different big contract to make it work, so be it.

He got out to an uncharacteristically rough start to the 2026 campaign. But Abreu was one of the best relievers in all of baseball from 2022-25, and he gave the Astros a 1.87 ERA over his final 44 appearances.

He's still only 29 years old, and if you take out his first 11 appearances of this season, he has a 2.28 ERA over the past half-decade. No one with at least 300 innings of work during that time can boast a mark that low.

Abreu should be headed for a closer role, but maybe the Dodgers make it worth his while to stick to the seventh and eighth innings.

Per MLB.com's pipeline rankings , the Dodgers have five of the top 33 prospects in baseball.

They also have a surplus of starting pitching, even if we disregard free agents Tarik Skubal, Kris Bubic and Eric Lauer. At any rate, they could trade away Bobby Miller, Landon Knack, Gavin Stone and Emmet Sheehan and still have a solid six-man rotation. (Assuming Shohei Ohtani returns to pitching in 2027.)

In other words, if any team has a stack of trade chips big enough to entice Cincinnati into at least answering a phone call about Elly De La Cruz, it's the Dodgers.

It'd be pretty funny if Mike Sirota was one of the biggest chips in that offer, considering the Reds gave that now top prospect to the Dodgers two winters ago for Gavin Lux. But if they can get De La Cruz at shortstop and slide Mookie Betts back to second base, that sure would make it tougher to find a weakness in this roster.

Durán broke out in a huge way this season, providing more value than any other Ranger while playing anywhere and everywhere in the field. He's probably going to win the AL Gold Glove for utility players.

He has two years of arbitration eligibility remaining and could be the perfect solution to the question of whether Miguel Rojas is going to come back for one more year at the age of 38.

Gilbert has just one year of arbitration eligibility remaining, and he's probably going to cost around $16M-$17M.

The Mariners certainly don't have to trade him away. Unloading Luis Castillo's contract onto the White Sox over the summer sure did make it easier for them to justify hanging onto Gilbert.

But with Kade Anderson arriving late in the year and Emerson Hancock having a breakout season, it's very likely that Seattle will at least entertain the possibility of turning Gilbert into a top prospect and reallocating that $16M-$17M to a free agent bat that might actually help them bounce back in 2027.

And if the Dodgers are concerned in any way about Ohtani's availability as a pitcher next year, a one-year rental of Gilbert would be quite the insurance policy.

Starting Lineup (vs. Atlanta Braves LHP Chris Sale)

And on multiple levels, the Dodgers ain't broke.

They'll do something about losing Miguel Rojas. We shall see whether that's signing someone like Brandon Lowe or Jazz Chisholm Jr. to man second base so Tommy Edman can serve as the super utilityman or just signing a new utilityman like Mauricio Dubón, but that will likely be their only significant move among the position players.

On the mound, Tarik Skubal is the colossal domino. And if the Dodgers aren't the singular favorite to sign him, they are surely on the short list of candidates with the spending power to do so.

Just to switch things up, though, let's assume for a change that Los Angeles doesn't sign the best pitcher available this winter.

It's still a preposterously loaded staff, as evidenced by the fact that we can't even find room for the likes of Bobby Miller, Landon Knack, Will Klein and Kyle Hurt, while also needing to choose between Emmet Sheehan and Roki Sasaki for the No. 6 spot in the rotation.

Inevitably, there will be injuries. It's why the Dodgers have made it a point to have at least 10 viable starting pitchers on their payroll over the past few years. But as things presently stand—with not a single pitcher already on the 2027 shelf for Tommy John recovery—they sure are deep and looking like the preseason favorites yet again.

articles.body:
Shohei Ohtani and the Los Angeles Dodgers were eliminated from the 2026 MLB postseason with a 6-4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the NLCS on Thursday night.

The Dodgers were swept by the Brewers as their quest for a third consecutive World Series title came to an end.

Here's a look at how Ohtani fared during Los Angeles' playoff run:

Yankees higher ups annoyed with Aaron Judge

The four-time MVP hit a three-run home run on Thursday, but struggled throughout the majority of the postseason.

Ohtani only finished with a .631 OPS in the playoffs, representing a steep drop compared to his career OPS of .948.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts considered benching Ohtani due to his struggles as well as his overall injury concerns after Milwaukee took a 2-0 series lead in the NLCS, but ultimately kept him in the lineup.

It's worth noting that the 32-year-old missed just over two weeks before the start of the playoffs due to lingering left knee and right biceps injuries . Ohtani previously stopped pitching in July after dealing with left knee inflammation .

Still, his overall performance was disappointing after he operated as a key piece of Los Angeles' batting order during its World Series victories in 2024 and 2025.

In 34 combined playoff games across those two seasons, Ohtani racked up 11 homers and 24 RBI to go along with a .248/.390/.550 slash line.

He wasn't able to maintain a similar level of production this year, though.

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani hits Dodgers' first and only homer of NLCS, and his first since Aug. 18, after move back to leadoff spot
articles.summary: Shohei Ohtani needed that.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers batted Shohei Ohtani second, fourth, fifth and sixth in their lineup across their first seven games this postseason. Down 3-0 in the National League Championship Series, they had one more idea for him.

It worked out in the second inning, but in a losing effort .

The Dodgers returned Ohtani to the leadoff spot for Game 4 and were rewarded with a two-out, three-run homer that gave them a 4-0 lead in the second inning. He took a low cutter from Brewers starter Dustin May and crushed it 428 feet for his first homer since Aug. 18.

It was the Dodgers' first home run of the series, and no one was more pumped than Ohtani. It's hard to think of another time the usually reserved slugger was this visibly excited.

Those wound up being the Dodgers' final runs of the season, as the Brewers proceeded to throw seven scoreless innings while coming back for a 6-4 win. With the sweep, they advance to their first World Series since 1982, while the Dodgers fall eight wins short of a three-peat.

Shohei Ohtani's homer came after a month of struggles

Ohtani was the Dodgers' every-day leadoff hitter from June 2024 until September of this year. Due to struggles related to knee, biceps and neck injuries, the Dodgers placed him on the injured list in September, then put him in a leadoff platoon with Betts when he returned for the final five games of the season.

However, Ohtani struggled mightily after coming back from the IL, which resulted in him moving further back in the batting order until he was hitting sixth in Game 3 on Wednesday, his lowest placement since before his first MVP year in 2021 .

Ohtani, who was adamant about continuing to play, did have a decent game Wednesday, going 1-for-2 with a single, walk and hit-by-pitch. That was apparently enough to convince the Dodgers to give leadoff another try.

Here's Dodgers manager Dave Roberts' pregame explanation:

"Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at. I like the at-bats yesterday, and I felt that trying to shake it up a bit — obviously, we haven't performed the way that we're capable of. Something that's of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to."

Ohtani's placement was ultimately a small button to press, but the Dodgers were at the point where they would try anything. Their offense, one of the best in baseball during the regular season, went dormant in the NLCS after barely showing up in the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves.

Dodgers hitters entered Game 4 hitting 3-for-32 with runners in scoring position in the postseason, with zero home runs this series. You can ascribe that to basic bad luck, a lack of execution from a veteran-heavy group, clutch performance by the Brewers (and Braves) pitchers or some sort of Space Jam-esque talent robbery, but it all added up to a unit that needed a change.

Ohtani, as he has so many times in the past, delivered on that front in the second inning. Unfortunately, more of the same followed, as the Dodgers finished the game 2-for-11 with RISP.

articles.title: Brewers roar back from 4 runs down to sweep Dodgers, reach first World Series since 1982
articles.summary: There will be no three-peat for the Dodgers.
articles.body: There will be no three-peat for the Los Angeles Dodgers. Instead, it will be the Milwaukee Brewers' first World Series appearance since 1982.The Brewers completed an NLCS sweep of the defending champions with a 6-4 comeback win in Game 4 on Thursday, delivering the exact opposite of their own sweep at the hands of the Dodgers in the 2025 NLCS. The Brewers will face either the Cleveland Guardians or the Tampa Bay Rays as they go for the first World Series title in franchise history.“For the first time in 44 years, the @Brewers are going to the World Series!"@MLBONFOX pic.twitter.com/XnL14R3bGF— FOX Sports (@FOXSports) October 16, 2026 Game 1 of the Fall Classic is scheduled for Friday, Oct. 23, giving Milwaukee a full week of rest, while the Guardians lead the Rays 2-1 in the ALCS.Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers, who delivered huge moments in Games 2, 3 and 4, was named NLCS MVP. That's pretty good for a guy who might have retired two years ago had his pregnant wife not needed health insurance.The Dodgers entered Thursday in need of a nearly unprecedented comeback, with only one team in history having successfully come back from down 3-0 in a seven-game series. That team, the 2004 Boston Red Sox, famously included Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, but that was more of a fun quirk of history than a meaningful reason for confidence in Los Angeles.As it turned out, the only comeback was in favor of the Brewers, who found themselves down 4-0 in the second inning after Shohei Ohtani hit the Dodgers' first — and only — home run of the series. If the Dodgers were going to do the nearly impossible, it was a good start, especially for a player who hadn't homered since Aug. 18.But as cathartic as that moment seemed, with Ohtani flipping his bat and nearly losing his mind as he walked past the plate, the Brewers barely blinked.Milwaukee instead did what it has done all series and all season. It got guys on base and made them move. The fourth inning saw Bauers hit a two-run double to cut the deficit in half.Jake Bauers cannot be stopped!He cuts the Brewers deficit in half 💪 pic.twitter.com/AklAZgtDqV— MLB (@MLB) October 16, 2026 The fifth inning saw a series of walks that culminated in Bauers drawing a four-pitch free pass with the bases loaded to tie the game.Jake Bauers draws a bases-loaded walk!TIE GAME! pic.twitter.com/zeZgMPkMVG— MLB (@MLB) October 16, 2026 And the sixth inning saw Garrett Mitchell crush a solo homer to center field to give the Brewers the lead for good.GARRETT MITCHELL!THE BREWERS HAVE COME ALL THE WAY BACK TO TAKE THE LEAD! pic.twitter.com/dOx9zZUHT7— MLB (@MLB) October 16, 2026 In 286 career regular-season games, Mitchell has two total home runs against left-handed pitchers. He posted homers against southpaws, Blake Snell and Alex Vesia, in Games 3 and 4.David Hamilton, the NL leader in sacrifice bunts this season, added another solo homer in the ninth inning. The point of the Brewers might as well be that anyone can do anything. Anyone can get on base. Anyone can break through for sudden power. On the mound, anyone can deliver multiple quality innings. Throughout the series, they were the more complete team.The Dodgers, meanwhile, picked a very bad time for their offense to misfire like a rocket operated by Wile E. Coyote.Ohtani's homer was one of two hits with runners in scoring position in that inning, but that was the only time the Dodgers delivered multiple such hits in a game the entire postseason. Overall, they went 5-for-43 in that regard between the NLDS and NLCS.Combine that with an overall power outage — the Brewers out-homered them 7-1 in this series — and there were no paths for L.A. to make this a series. A lineup of well-paid veteran hitters with considerable past postseason success simply wilted.AARON ASHBY ESCAPES AGAIN!3 OUTS AWAY! pic.twitter.com/63nuErorT2— MLB (@MLB) October 16, 2026 The Brewers' pitching staff deserves credit for much of that. Dustin May began his appearance with a stumble, but recovered to finish three innings without further issue. JoJo Romero recorded two more scoreless innings, followed by Aaron Ashby once again delivering three scoreless innings in the clutch.The Brewers were the best team of the 2026 regular season, and they have been the best team of the postseason through three rounds. If they can win one more round, they will accomplish the one thing their fans have been waiting for decades to see.

articles.title: Dodgers veteran Miguel Rojas pulled before first at-bat in final game of 13-year career
articles.summary: The Dodgers' 2025 postseason hero was pulled in the second inning of their final game of 2026.
articles.body:
As planned, Los Angeles Dodgers veteran Miguel Rojas will retire after the 2026 season. Unfortunately for him, the 2026 season hardly ended the way the Dodgers had planned.

Rojas got the start in Game 4, playing second base and batting seventh in what he later confirmed was the final game of his career . He played two innings of defense and was due to hit in the bottom of the second when a curious sequence of events saw him get pulled before his first at-bat.

Kyle Tucker led off the second inning with a single, which prompted the Brewers to pull left-handed opener Shane Drohan for right-hander Dustin May. May then allowed another single to Teoscar Hernández.

With runners on first and second and a chance to draw first blood, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts opted to pinch-hit the left-handed Max Muncy for the right-handed Rojas, who usually starts only against southpaws.

And that's how Rojas' career ended. Muncy went on to strike out, but the Dodgers scored their four runs on a subsequent single from Andy Pages and homer from Shohei Ohtani .

Rojas' confirmation after the game, via Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times :

"This is it as a player. That was my last game played. That was the last time I put these cleats on and this uniform on as a player … I'm ready to move on and start the next chapter of my career."

It's a disappointing ending for Rojas, though the Dodgers obviously had bigger concerns in an elimination game. Rojas had to understand what was coming, as part of the point of an opener is to force teams to pull their platoon bats or face disadvantageous matchups for the rest of the game.

Nothing will erase what Rojas did as a player, though. He spent 13 years as a defensive standout for the Dodgers and Miami Marlins, but it's what he did as a hitter in the 2025 World Series that will be most remembered in baseball history. With the Dodgers down to their final two outs in Game 7 against the Toronto Blue Jays, Rojas hit a game-tying solo homer to force extra innings.

Rojas said last postseason he intended to retire after 2026 and opted to return to the Dodgers on a one-year, $5.5 million deal . That contract came with a plan for him to join the Dodgers in a player development role after his retirement.

Rojas confirmed that's still his intention:

"From now on, I'm going to start thinking about what's going to happen in my life as a baseball person, other than being a player. I want to start my career on the other side of this business and I'm looking forward to doing it here with the Los Angeles Dodgers."

Rojas' professional career dates back to 2006, when he signed with the Cincinnati Reds out of Venezuela. He didn't make his MLB debut until eight years later, when he debuted with the Dodgers after signing a minor-league deal. He proceeded to carve out a bench role before he was traded to the Marlins in a deal that included future teammate Kiké Hernández going to LA.

articles.title: Brewers Manager Pat Murphy Takes Shot at Dodgers After Win
articles.summary: Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy took a shot at the Los Angeles Dodgers after they swept them in the National League Championship Series.In what was an u...
articles.body:
Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy took a shot at the Los Angeles Dodgers after they swept them in the National League Championship Series.

In what was an upset, the Brewers defeated the Dodgers 6-4 in Game 4 on Thursday night at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles to sweep the best-of-seven series 4-0.

The Brewers now await the winner of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and the Tampa Bay Rays. The Guardians currently have a 2-1 lead in that best-of-seven series.

Speaking after his young, scrappy, and lower-payroll Brewers team won the NL pennant, Murphy — the reigning two-time NL Manager of the Year — took a shot at the Dodgers and their expensive roster of All-Star veterans.

"They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we have a bunch of gamers, and the gamers won this week," Murphy said.

Brewers Payroll Lagged in Comparison to Dodgers

Per The Sporting News, the Dodgers had the No. 2 payroll in MLB this season at $339.32 million, while the Brewers were 19th at $146.21 million. However, the Dodgers also had several players on deferred salaries, and they are paying a massive amount of money in luxury tax, so the financial gap is even greater between these two ballclubs.

However, the Brewers still managed to dethrone the Dodgers, who had won the last two World Series trophies in MLB. This was akin to David topping Goliath in many ways, and there are likely many fans outside of Los Angeles tonight who are thrilled that this lower-payroll Brewers ballclub was able to not only defeat the pricey Dodgers, but sweep them.

Now, the Brewers will be looking to win the first World Series in franchise history when they take on either the Guardians or the Rays in this year's finals.

Since that series is still ongoing for at least a few more days, the Brewers will be able to get a little bit of rest before they enter the World Series, which could allow their arms to recover as Milwaukee and Murphy look to capture the 2026 MLB World Series trophy this postseason.

articles.title: Miguel Rojas announces retirement after Brewers sweep Dodgers in NLCS
articles.summary: LOS ANGELES — Miguel Rojas stood in the Los Angeles Dodgers clubhouse Thursday night, still wearing the uniform he had proudly worn for the past four seasons...
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES — Miguel Rojas stood in the Los Angeles Dodgers clubhouse Thursday night, still wearing the uniform he had proudly worn for the past four seasons, knowing he would never put it on again as a player.

The Dodgers' season had just ended in disappointing fashion, with the Milwaukee Brewers completing a four-game sweep in the National League Championship Series. For Rojas, however, the loss marked more than the end of another postseason run. It was the end of his playing career.

The veteran infielder announced his retirement following the Dodgers' elimination, confirming that he had played his final Major League Baseball game and was ready to begin the next chapter of his life in baseball, preferably with the organization that helped him finish his career as a two-time World Series champion.

"No, I think this is it, guys," Rojas said after the game. "This is it as a player. That was my last game played. That was the last time that I put these cleats on and this uniform on as a player. From now on, I'm going to start thinking about what's going to happen in my life as a baseball person."

Rojas said he hopes to remain with the Dodgers in a coaching or organizational role, continuing a relationship that has become one of the most meaningful parts of his professional and personal life.

"I want to start my career on the other side of this business, and I'm looking forward to doing it here with the Los Angeles Dodgers as well," Rojas said. "It's really hard because I never wanted to make a big conference or anything like that, but I just wanted to be clear with the guys and with everybody in this clubhouse. This was it, so I'm ready to move on and start the next chapter of my career."

The announcement came after an emotional clubhouse meeting in which Dodgers manager Dave Roberts gave Rojas an opportunity to address his teammates one final time as a player.

Rather than focusing on the disappointment of losing to Milwaukee or the opportunity that had slipped away to win a third consecutive World Series championship, Rojas used the moment to thank the teammates, coaches and organization that had helped transform his life.

"Doc gave me the opportunity to talk to the group," Rojas said. "I just said thank you because it changed my life. I truly and honestly say that from the bottom of my heart. The last couple of years here for me, it's been the most amazing time of my life in baseball. And I grew so much with this group. I grew as a man, as a father, as a player, as a leader, as a teammate."

Rojas, who began his major league career with the Dodgers in 2014 before spending eight seasons with the Miami Marlins, returned to Los Angeles in 2023 and became an important part of the team's clubhouse leadership.

While his contributions on the field were valuable, particularly his defensive versatility and ability to play multiple infield positions, Rojas established himself as one of the most respected voices in a clubhouse filled with superstars.

He helped guide the Dodgers through consecutive championship seasons in 2024 and 2025, providing veteran leadership alongside players such as Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and Yoshinobu Yamamoto.

Rojas also delivered one of the most memorable moments of the Dodgers' championship run in 2025, hitting a dramatic ninth-inning home run in Game 7 of the World Series against the Toronto Blue Jays. The home run helped keep the Dodgers' championship hopes alive before they eventually secured their second consecutive title.

That moment will forever be part of Dodgers postseason history, but Rojas said his greatest memories extend far beyond any single play or championship celebration.

"The last four years here for me have changed my life," Rojas said. "I couldn't be more proud of being a Los Angeles Dodger for the time that I was here. And I promised the guys loyalty forever because they helped me grow. And not just as a player, but as a person, as a leader, as a future coach or whatever my job is going to be in the future as a baseball man."

The emotions were especially difficult Thursday because Rojas had spent the previous two seasons celebrating championships with his teammates. This time, there would be no champagne celebration or championship parade. Instead, there were hugs, farewells and the realization that an extraordinary chapter had come to an end.

"I never thought about this moment when I was playing because I always thought it was going to be the next game," Rojas said. "But right now, with everything that happened, I think it helped me close the chapter and helped me close my career the way that I never envisioned happening."

Rojas acknowledged that the Brewers deserved credit for ending the Dodgers' pursuit of a historic three-peat. Milwaukee dominated the series and consistently delivered in the biggest moments, something Rojas said separated the two teams.

"They were really good," Rojas said. "All credit to the Brewers, the organization, everything that they did these last four games against us. It was to perfection. From Pat Murphy and the guys winning moments, I think that's what a championship team does. They got the big hit when they needed, they got the big out when they needed, and we got beat. There's nothing else that we can say. We were prepared, we were ready, and it wasn't just our series, it was their series."

Despite the disappointing conclusion to the season, Rojas rejected the idea that the Dodgers' championship window was closing.

With Ohtani, Betts, Freeman and Yamamoto remaining at the center of the organization, Rojas believes Los Angeles will continue competing for championships long after his playing days are over.

"I feel like the talent in this organization is so broad that you can't really think about this being the end of our era on the Dodgers," Rojas said. "I know this organization so well that they're not going to be satisfied with this loss, and I think they're going to move forward and they're going to continue to improve the team in any capacity. And I believe that we're going to be even better next year."

When asked what he would remember most about playing alongside Ohtani, Rojas pointed not to the superstar's extraordinary accomplishments but to his commitment to showing up every day, regardless of the pressure or expectations surrounding him.

"What I respect the most is he's always ready to play baseball," Rojas said. "He's always ready to show up for his team and for his teammates. The weight of the world is kind of on his shoulders every single night for him to perform. And even when he struggled, he always wanted to put his uniform on and go out there every single day for his teammates and for everybody who's following. So that's something that I will remember from him."

For Rojas, the relationships built inside the Dodgers clubhouse have become as meaningful as the championships themselves. He spoke emotionally about the impact the organization has had on his family, including his son and daughter, and how the past four seasons have prepared him for whatever comes next.

"I told them thank you because they changed my life the last four years here," Rojas said. "Not just because of me, but my family, my son, my daughter. They made me grow as a player, but they also made me grow as a leader."

Rojas said he hopes the culture he helped establish in Los Angeles will continue after his departure from the active roster. Although his role will change, his loyalty to the organization will not.

He also understands that very few players get to finish their careers exactly as they envision. While he would have preferred to walk away after another World Series championship, Rojas takes comfort in knowing that he was part of something special in Los Angeles.

"There's a lot of things to be happy for and to be proud of," Rojas said. "Being part of this group and trying to win three times in a row, it was special. And that's something that I'm going to remember forever. The good, the bad, the ups and downs, it's all part of the process and it's all part of the journey."

As he prepared to take off his Dodgers uniform for the final time as a player, Rojas reflected on the championships that will forever connect him with his teammates and the organization.

"No one can take away from us what we did the last two years being champions," Rojas said. "That makes me so proud that we're going to cherish that bond forever. And this one feels really bad, but at the end of the day, we're always going to have something that we can share together, which is championships."

For Rojas, Thursday night marked the end of his playing career, but perhaps not the end of his time with the Dodgers. The veteran infielder hopes to remain a familiar face around the clubhouse, only next time in a different role, helping the next generation of players chase the same championships that defined the final years of his career.

articles.title: What happened in Dodgers clubhouse after season-ending loss to Brewers?
articles.summary: The Dodgers came up short of their goal to wins three straight World Series titles and they shared their thoughts after getting swept by the Brewers.
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES — The tears had mostly dried in the Los Angeles Dodgers clubhouse.

About 30 minutes had elapsed after the Dodgers got swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series. Their hopes for a third straight World Series title officially died with a 6 -4 defeat Thursday, Oct. 15 at Dodger Stadium .

What had taken place before those clubhouse doors opened to the media?

Miguel Rojas, the Dodgers' veteran second baseman, looked misty-eyed. He is retiring and expressed gratitude to the team because his years with the Dodgers organization changed his life – not just as a player, but as a husband and father.

He said he received emotional hugs from teammates, with Rojas headed into retirement.

Max Muncy, the Dodgers' third baseman, referred to unseen emotion.

"Right now we're trying to soak in what we got in this clubhouse," he said. "We're all trying to tell each other that we love each other and thank each other. There's going to come a time where we'll worry about next year, but it's just right not now."

Best ALCS and NLCS photos from the 2026 MLB playoffs

Ohtani told reporters he doesn't know if he'll need surgery for the knee and bicep issues that limited his pitching and led to a horrendous hitting slump.

"I haven't been able to come to grips with what I learned overall this season," Ohtani said after the game. "I will go back to the drawing board in terms of treatment, a training program and see what I can come up with for next season. … And looking forward to having a better season next year."

The Brewers looked spry as they sped around the basepaths. Not the Dodgers.

Ohtani, 32, still has seven years left on his 10-year, $700 million deal. Mookie Betts is under contract through 2032. But Freddie Freeman and Max Muncy, both among the older Dodgers, have only one year left on their contracts.

Freeman, the 37-year-old All-Star first baseman, is among the more grizzled Dodgers. He smiled as reporters clustered around his locker and referred to remarks that Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made in the clubhouse before those doors opened.

"Obviously came in pretty hurt, down," Freeman said. "But (Roberts) said some encouraging things. Sport is rough sometimes when you go out there and give it your all. Sometimes you come up short, but that's life."

But the philosophical will be competing with the numerical.

A hypothetical MLB salary cap could force the Dodgers to work under financial constraints for the first time since Mark Walter and his partners bought the team in 2012 for $2.15 million.

The most striking emotion from the Dodgers came during the game. It was the shouting and gesticulating after Ohtani hit a three-run homer in the second inning.

It was his first home run since Aug. 18, and as the ball sailed over the right-field wall Ohtani turned toward the Dodgers' dugout, raised his arms and yelled.

"I think it was a lot of pent-up anger, frustration. It was the best ball he hit in probably two, three months, and it was a big hit," Roberts said. "For him to look at the dugout, show that emotion, it just shows how much he cares. He's still human. He still cares and wants to help his team win a baseball game."

Ohtani looked serene in the clubhouse as he appeared in front of his locker with his translator.

Maybe it's best to finish with the starter.

Dodgers righthander Tyler Glasnow retired the first nine Brewers hitters in a row and had six strikeouts. Los Angeles had jumped to a 4-0 lead.

But less than two innings later he'd been pulled from the game and the Brewers had tied the score 4-4.

"I just think they played a lot better than us," Glasnow said, looking despondent in front of his locker. "They were hitting on everything and I just think it wasn't our year."

Over that, there's still time for the Dodgers to shed a few more tears.

articles.title: Not even a Shohei Ohtani resurgence is enough as Dodgers fall to Brewers in unthinkable NLCS sweep
articles.summary: The back-to-back champs exited the postseason an incomprehensibly woeful 5-for-43 with runners in scoring position.
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES — Shohei Ohtani took two small steps toward home plate.

For an entire second, the sporting supernova believed he would get at least one more opportunity to reorient the most disappointing month of his professional life. As the baseball thundered off Kiké Hernández's bat toward left-center field at 107.9 mph, Dodger Stadium, too, felt a flicker of hope. The optimism was warranted: It was the hardest ball Hernández had struck all season. If pearl met grass, Ohtani would come to the plate as the tying run in this knife's-edge NLCS Game 4 .

There was a window, it seemed, as left fielder Jackson Chourio raced into the gap.

Surely, Ohtani yearned for that shot, a shot to once again spark his sluggish goliath of a ballclub, currently trailing the relentless Milwaukee Brewers three games to zero. The road back to glory, even with an L.A. victory on Thursday, would be long and steep and imposing. But only with another moment of magic from the injured and beleaguered four-time MVP could the Dodgers even begin to consider the impossible.

Chourio leapt into the air. The line drive clattered into his mitt. He let out a joyous roar, never breaking stride. Milwaukee's finest poured out of the first-base dugout onto the diamond, grabbing one another in disbelief. Chavez Ravine — the parts not from Wisconsin, anyway — snapped to a hush.

Ohtani strode back toward the dugout, toward winter, toward questions, toward home.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

The 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers, the most expensive baseball team ever assembled , ended their season with a 6-4 loss on Thursday . Approximately $433 million, suddenly, shockingly, on vacation. Ultimately, the Dodgers proved too old, too tired, too slow. Their star-studded pitching staff was not quite sharp enough to overcome those shortcomings. Their slug-reliant offense melted with runners in scoring position. Game 4 then, a nail-biting delight of a contest, was a beautiful microcosm of that dynamic.

As always, the story revolved around Ohtani. Injured and depleted for this entire postseason, he'd been reinserted in the leadoff spot by manager Dave Roberts after looking somewhat rejuvenated in Game 3.

"I think the player still has to give you hope — like to believe in, to bet on," Roberts explained regarding his renewed faith in Ohtani after dropping him to sixth in the lineup on Wednesday. "I feel good about him taking five at-bats and giving us our best chance to win and produce runs today."

In his second at-bat of Game 4, producing runs is exactly what Ohtani did.

With the Dodgers already up a run in the second inning, with two on and two out, the lefty slugger absolutely unstitched a bottom-rail cutter from Dustin May into the right-field bleachers. Ohtani watched it fly for a half-beat as May crumpled to his knees, then turned back toward his dugout, threw his arms apart, pumped his fist and let loose a cathartic yell. It was quite the emotional display from the typically even-keeled character. Call it whatever you want — redemption, release, sporting absolution — but the box score called it a homer, Ohtani's first since Aug. 18.

"It was just good to see him hit a ball hard," Mookie Betts said postgame. "When it went over the fence, I think from that point, we knew we were going to be in a good spot."

And for about an hour, with a four-run cushion, that's where Ohtani, Betts and Co. were: a good spot.

For just the second time all series, Milwaukee failed to score in the half-inning following a Los Angeles run. Dodgers starter Tyler Glasnow retired the first 10 batters he faced, notching six strikeouts. The skeptical home crowd bought in. A tangible buzz began to build. With two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal slated for Game 5 and October icon Yoshinobu Yamamoto set for Game 6, a roadmap started to reveal itself. Maybe the Dodgers could actually do this.

In the fourth, NLCS MVP Jake Bauers laced a full-count ground-rule double to plate a pair. One inning later, the Brewers tied things up on a David Hamilton RBI single and a bases-loaded walk drawn by, of course, Bauers. Meanwhile, Los Angeles' lineup threw things back into cruise control, collecting just one total baserunner across the third, fourth and fifth. Tension and doubt, its evil cousin, inched back across the crowd.

Milwaukee center fielder Garrett Mitchell then gave that crowd a souvenir, clocking a go-ahead heat-seeker in the top of the sixth off reliever Tanner Scott. It was Mitchell's second left-on-left long ball in the past two games. He hit one in the regular season.

At that point, 12 outs remained between the Brewers and the pennant. Twelve outs stood between the Dodgers and the unthinkable.

Trailing by just one run, Los Angeles' collection of high-priced hitters placed a runner at third base in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings. Each time, they failed to score.

Bespectacled Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby had a lot to do with that. In the seventh, with one out and the tying run at third, the flamethrowing southpaw sat Ohtani down on three straight pitches. The final perplexer, a devastating slider in the right-handed batter's box, left Ohtani flailing at air.

"The Brewers were overall strong and a very good team, and they really exposed some of the parts of me as a player, and I give some credit to themm" Ohtani said postgame via interpreter Will Ireton.

While strolling back to the dugout after that Ashby at-bat, not to hit again this season, Ohtani banged his helmet with his right hand in frustration. As he did so, Betts' walk-up song bumped from the speakers: "It's a whole lotta money in this motherf***er."

Sure is, not that Ashby cared. The next inning, he elicited a harmless pop-up from Kyle Tucker, the highest paid soul in the sport, with the tying run once again on third.

And there went the 2026 Dodgers, an incomprehensibly woeful 5-for-43 with runners in scoring position in this postseason, once again unable to cash in.

"We just didn't come through in a couple of those situations. That's a part of the game," Betts lamented afterward. "Everybody's trying. Everybody's doing their best. Sometimes your best isn't good enough."

The truth for the Dodgers, cemented by Hernández's unlucky laser in the ninth, might be even more humbling than that.

Baseball itself, in the year since Los Angeles' dominant sweep of these Brewers in the 2025 NLCS, evolved enough to make the Dodgers' style of play look antiquated, even dusty. During the regular season, Los Angeles had the third-slowest team bat speed in MLB and the second-lowest hard-swing rate. They ranked 25th in team sprint speed; Milwaukee ranked 1st.

From Aug. 18, the date of Ohtani's last regular-season long ball, the allegedly contact-merchant Brewers hit just three fewer homers than the Dodgers. Even where the 100-win Dodgers shined, the 103-win Brewers topped them. The only team with a higher average fastball velocity than Los Angeles in these playoffs? Milwaukee. The game is quicker now, and the Dodgers, so long the cutting-edge force in the sport, failed to keep up.

Not even the brief reappearance of a full-bore Ohtani was enough to bridge the gap. That he ended the season on-deck, with his teammates unable to get him that fifth at-bat Roberts had planned for, only dumped salt in the wound. So close, yet so far. Four wins away — or eight, in fact.

While the 2026 team is finished playing ball, don't expect the Dodgers, and all they mean, to exit the conversation. Beneath the specter of a looming labor fight , Los Angeles' gilded roster will remain in the spotlight even once autumn flips to winter. But their being bested in this particular series has less to do with larger debates about the game's future or economics and more with the simple fact that a superior Brewers team kicked their doors in. On the field, this was not an underdog story or an upset.

articles.title: Dodgers’ Kiké Hernandez keeps it 100% real on not being able to ‘out-talent’ Brewers in NLCS
articles.summary: Everything was looking good for the Los Angeles Dodgers heading into the 2026 MLB postseason, at least on paper. But teams play games on the field, not on pa...
articles.body:
Everything was looking good for the Los Angeles Dodgers heading into the 2026 MLB postseason, at least on paper. But teams play games on the field, not on paper. The Milwaukee Brewers made quick work of them in the 2026 NLCS, sending them home after just four games by taking a 6-4 victory on Thursday night in Game 4 to complete the sweep.

The Dodgers have the second-biggest payroll in MLB, and they have superstars up and down the roster. And yet they couldn't even win one postseason game against a Brewers team that spent nearly $200 million fewer in player payroll this season. At the end of the day, the Dodgers know that the Brewers simply outplayed them, as Kiké Hernandez so succinctly put .

"It's really hard to win in this sport. Sometimes you can't always out-talent people. You've got to play the game and play better than the other team. That's what happened in this series," Hernandez said, per Bill Plunkett of the Orange County Register.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Indeed, the Brewers came up with the runs when it mattered the most, while the Dodgers couldn't make their opportunities count. This could not have been more apparent than in Game 4.

After the Brewers had taken the lead, 5-4, in the top of the sixth thanks to a Garrett Mitchell solo homer , the Dodgers put the tying run on base in three consecutive innings — failing to drive them in on every opportunity.

By the time the bottom of the ninth came along, it was already too late for the Dodgers. The Brewers had padded their lead with a solo shot from David Hamilton , and Hernandez hit the final out of the game, sending a sharp liner to deep left field — only for Jackson Chourio to catch the ball on the run to secure the sweep for Milwaukee.

The Dodgers' position player core is aging, and they have some injury problems to navigate, particularly with Shohei Ohtani . They will surely sign reinforcements to bolster the roster, but it won't matter at the end of the day if they can't get it done on the diamond.

articles.title: After a failed World Series attempt, Dodgers are left wondering what happened to their season, and their star
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Dodgers’ push to win a third straight World Series ended officially Thursday, swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series. Lack of production from their superstar is a reason why.
articles.body: The Los Angeles Dodgers’ push to win a third straight World Series ended officially Thursday, swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series. Their chances were never the same, however, as early as June. The Dodgers started June 11 the way they began the season — as a heavy favorite to become the first franchise since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees to claim three consecutive championships. Their active roster, the most expensive in the sport, included two former World Series MVPs, one Cy Young winner, and a second would be added a few weeks later at the trade deadline. The linchpin was superstar Shohei Ohtani, the four-time MVP whose pitching and hitting feats were unparalleled in modern baseball history, and had helped the club win titles in each of his first two seasons in Los Angeles. That version of Ohtani was on display June 11 in Pittsburgh. He started the day with a minuscule 1.06 ERA in 11 appearances on the mound. Against the Pirates, he proceeded to hit a solo homer and get on base in all four plate appearances. Then, in the seventh inning, Ohtani exited with what the team called knee inflammation. The injury appeared innocuous. It was instead the first in a series of lingering knee and bicep injuries that diminished Ohtani and eventually derailed the Dodgers juggernaut (total payroll cost: $339 million) until they couldn’t keep up with Milwaukee ($146 million), which clinched its sweep with Thursday’s 6-4 win in Los Angeles. After exiting the June 11 game in Pittsburgh, Ohtani pitched only three more times and had an ERA of 4.50 before being shut down as a pitcher July 3. The Dodgers’ postseason disappointment could not be explained alone by Ohtani’s decline over the season’s back half. The Dodgers’ bullpen and vaunted starters also showed vulnerabilities throughout the summer. Yet, when the rest of the team’s offense sputtered for long stretches, Ohtani’s inability to rescue his team at the plate was even more pronounced. The Dodgers hit .257 during the regular season to just .188 in the postseason. Their OPS, a measure of both on-base percentage and slugging, ranked second-best during the season (.762). In the playoffs, that average fell to .572. “They just out-pitched us, they outhit us, they played defense better, they didn’t make any mistakes,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told Fox after Game 4. Ohtani produced just one RBI in his final 83 plate appearances of the regular season, a stretch that included 11 hits and 11 walks. Entering Thursday’s NLCS finale, Ohtani had gotten on base eight times in 28 postseason plate appearances, with his slugging percentage a fraction of his postseason career average. Desperate for a spark, the Dodgers moved Ohtani back into his traditional leadoff spot for Game 4 and he responded by hitting his first home run since Aug. 18, and driving in three runs. Ohtani tossed his bat and raised his arms to celebrate as the Dodgers took a 4-0 lead in the second inning. But just as it had been all season, as Ohtani went, so went the Dodgers. He never got on base again, and the Dodgers never scored again Thursday, allowing Milwaukee to recover and rally. The Dodgers aren’t the only ones in baseball entering this offseason facing uncertainty. A work stoppage is considered likely when the collective bargaining agreement between MLB and its players union expires Dec. 1. The league intends to address the wide financial gulf between their top-spending clubs and their thriftiest, despite the success of small-market teams this postseason. MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred has said the league wants to address “concerns that go to the core of what we’re about — that is competitive balance.” Backed by MLB’s richest TV deal, the Dodgers’ financial might allow them to build star-studded rosters that allowed them to withstand injuries and slumps by plugging in one promising player after another. That spending fueled their titles in 2020, 2024 and 2025 and should ensure they remain competitive for as long as owner Mark Walter intends to spend lavishly on the roster. Walter sold the Los Angeles Lakers and his stake in the Premier League club Chelsea to generate cash as federal investigators look into his businesses, but Dodgers leaders have maintained that Walter views the baseball club as a crown jewel of his portfolio of sports assets. “I can’t tell you how important the Dodgers are to Mark,” Dodgers executive Stan Kasten told reporters in August. Playing two ways is important to Ohtani. Yet, if there is baseball in 2027, Ohtani will be 33, and the combination of this season’s lingering injuries — to his knee, then his right biceps — and the team’s handling of them will place a spotlight on how willing the team is committed to using Ohtani as both a pitcher and hitter in future seasons. Rather than pull Ohtani from the lineup for a lengthy stretch until he was ready physically, the team deferred to the star’s feelings about his health, taking him out of the lineup for only a game or two throughout June, July and August. As recently as Game 3 of the NLCS this week, Roberts told reporters he’d had a “great conversation” with Ohtani and team executives in which Ohtani expressed a belief he was close to pulling out of a prodigious slump. “There’s just complete conviction that he’s onto something,” Roberts told reporters this week. “He feels like he can help us, and he can help us. For me, that’s all I need to hear.” Allowing a player’s input to influence their usage isn’t uncommon, but it has left the Dodgers relying on Ohtani’s candor. Though his health issues began cropping up in early June, it took until early September for the team to place Ohtani on the 15-day IL. “He’s not always the best reporter of how he feels,” Dodgers’ president of baseball operations, Andrew Friedman, said in late September. “Freddie (Freeman) is the same way, Clayton Kershaw, I’ve been around a lot of these guys that feel like their job is to be out there to help the team however they can and, sometimes, will downplay some things that are bothering them.” Before the Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves in the postseason divisional series, Ohtani told reporters that it had been difficult to get “a good grasp of the root cause of all this.” Before facing Milwaukee, Ohtani began taking batting practice outdoors, a rarity for a player who prefers to prepare inside batting cages under the stadium. “With the swing, it’s a daily process of trying different things,” Ohtani said last week. “The symptoms shouldn’t be the reason why I can’t hit.” In last year’s World Series, Ohtani had endured hitting slumps, too, but his teammates compensated with timely contributions to earn a second consecutive title. That was no longer the case this year. Of the 12 teams to reach the postseason, the Dodgers ranked 10th in OPS, a measure of both on-base percentage and slugging, while their pitchers ranked eighth in walks plus hits allowed per nine innings. After beating Atlanta to advance to the NLCS, the Dodgers wore celebratory T-shirts emblazoned with “Take October.” Unfortunately for them, their chance of a third consecutive World Series may as well have been taken out months earlier.
