articles.title: Ranking Dodgers SP Tarik Skubal's Top 5 Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Now that the Los Angeles Dodgers' season is over, it's time to begin playing what will be everyone's favorite game this winter: Where will Tarik Skubal sign?
articles.body:
Now that the Los Angeles Dodgers' season is over, it's time to begin playing what will be everyone's favorite game this winter: Where will Tarik Skubal sign?

It will be some time before we know the answer, but what we know for sure is that it's going to take several Brinks trucks to even get Skubal's and Scott Boras' attention. In a survey of industry insiders, Kiley McDaniel of ESPN found that the average projection for the lefty's next contract was eight years and $355 million.

Outrageous? Hardly. Skubal was the AL's Cy Young Award winner in 2024 and 2025. Elbow surgery and a modest decline this year took some of the shine off his left arm, but only so much. He still posted a 2.72 ERA and 6.89 K/BB ratio over 26 starts in the regular season, before further adding to an excellent playoff resume.

If Skubal and Boras do indeed shoot for a contract worth more than $300 million, there should be no mistake that his market will be limited. In all likelihood, we'll be able to count his realistic suitors on two hands or fewer.

Ahead, we'll break down five potential landing spots for Skubal and why they make sense for him.

The Angels may have lost 100 games for the first time in their history this year, but it wasn't because of their starting pitching. Their starters ranked in the top half of the league for ERA and rWAR.

Even if José Soriano is gone, Reid Detmers and Walbert Ureña are still around. If they find themselves pitching behind Skubal with top prospect Tyler Bremner waiting in the wings, suddenly the future doesn't look so bad.

As for the money question, this is a weird case where a team's incoming new owner isn't necessarily a better bet to break the bank than its soon-to-be former owner. Arte Moreno handed out more than his share of dumb money in his day. Stan Kroenke, by contrast, isn't known for doing that with his other teams.

It is nonetheless interesting that Skubal himself expects Kroenke to turn the Angels into a coveted destination for free agents . Provided Skubal is willing to wait until the sale of the franchise is final, perhaps he'll be willing to put… er, accept money where his mouth is.

The Padres weren't able to win the franchise's first World Series under the Seidler family. It wasn't for lack of trying, though, and new owners Kwanza Jones and José E. Feliciano don't sound interested in scaling back the effort.

"We need to win the World Series," Feliciano said in August . "It's that simple. That's what we're going to do."

If ever there was a way to show they mean business, it's by signing Skubal away from those darn Dodgers. Maybe it wouldn't totally undo the little brother vs. big brother dynamic between the two NL West powers, but it would give the Padres a real trump card: the best pitcher in baseball.

Besides, the Padres are going to need Skubal if Michael King declines his $28 million player option for 2027 and becomes a free agent. Skubal is one of the few pitchers in MLB who would represent an upgrade over King, even if signing him would likely cost more than $40 million per year.

Do the Yankees really need to go all-out for Skubal? Their starters led the majors with a 3.30 ERA this season, and all the main contributors are locked in for 2027 and beyond.

Well, sometimes the best thing to do with a strength is lean into it. And if the Yankees could line up Skubal with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón, that's when we could begin having the "Best Rotation Ever?" discussion.

As for the money, Hal Steinbrenner's limits are clearly lower than fans would (rightfully) like them to be. Despite still being the most valuable franchise in baseball, the Yankees tend to be more comfortable operating with MLB's No. 3 payroll than with its No. 1 payroll.

Of course, this doesn't mean the Yankees can't afford Skubal. Their roster already includes three players on contracts originally worth at least $300 million. And if Steinbrenner really wants to get serious about winning championship No. 28, a fourth should be in order.

Predicting 10 Biggest Contracts Handed Out to 2026-27 MLB Free Agents

Well, obviously the Dodgers are going to be a suitor for Skubal in free agency.

They are MLB's resident spending titan, but they don't have a ton of money set to come off their books this winter.

Then there's the uncertainty surrounding principal owner Mark Walter. The Athletic reported that Walter and insurance companies he controls were under federal investigation and that Walter and several companies had been named as defendants in a class-action lawsuit alleging fraud and other wrongdoing. Walter has also agreed to sell his Lakers stake, though Dodgers president and CEO Stan Kasten has said the Dodgers are not for sale. TWG Global has denied wrongdoing.

Until further notice, though, it's probably best to assume the Dodgers will keep acting like the Dodgers. Especially, that is, if they have reason to believe the next CBA is going to put checks on their power.

If so, this November is their chance for a last hurrah. Courting Skubal is their best way to make the most of that opportunity and, love it or hate it, extend a middle finger to the rest of the league.

The Mets are the top contender for Skubal because of course they are. Steve Cohen may not be MLB's richest owner anymore, but his track record speaks for itself.

Under him, the Mets have had MLB's No. 1 Opening Day payroll in three of the last four years. And while president of baseball operations David Stearns clearly falls on the risk-averse side , Cohen has been known to put his finger on the scale until it climbs all the way to $765 million .

That was for Juan Soto, of course, and there's no denying that the Mets need his equal on the mound. Their starting rotation was a disaster this year, ranking 23rd in ERA and rWAR.

Pairing Skubal with Nolan McLean won't fix that in one fell swoop, but it's the biggest possible step in the right direction.

articles.title: Predicting the 10 Biggest Contracts Handed Out to 2026-27 MLB Free Agents
articles.summary: The 2026-27 MLB free-agent class has a clear headliner in two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, but there's a significant drop-off behind him. The class as a whole lacks impact offensive talent.
articles.body:
The 2026-27 MLB free-agent class has a clear headliner in two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, but there's a significant drop-off behind him. The class as a whole lacks impact offensive talent.

Michael King, Freddy Peralta and Trevor Rogers are the top pitchers behind Skubal, while Randy Arozarena is the top bat on the market alongside Seiya Suzuki. After a down year, Jazz Chisholm Jr. might have to settle for a short-term, high-AAV deal as he looks to rebuild some value.

There is also a trio of Japanese League standouts in third baseman Teruaki Sato and pitchers Hiromi Itoh and Kaima Taira, who are expected to be posted. All three should command lucrative multi-year deals.

Ahead, we've taken a crack at predicting the 10 biggest contracts that will be handed out to the 2026-27 free-agent class this winter. A lot hinges on how things play out with the impending CBA negotiations and expected lockout, but for now, we'll treat our projections like any other offseason.

Age: 26 Stats: 23 GS, 12-5, 1.36 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 141 K, 146.0 IP

Used primarily as a reliever in Japan, right-hander Kaima Taira has also previously worked as a starter in 2023 (11-7, 2.40 ERA, 153 K, 150.0 IP) before returning to the rotation with fantastic results this past season.

With a 5'8", 209-pound frame, he might profile best in a bullpen role stateside, where his upper 90s fastball and wide array of secondary pitches could make him a multi-inning weapon or a closer.

Predicted Contract: 3 years, $60 million

The Astros gave Tatsuya Imai a three-year, $54 million deal last winter, betting on his stuff. Taira provides a similarly enticing repertoire. It might not be as straightforward as presented, with opt-outs and potential escalators for starts likely in play.

Age: 32 Stats: 634 PA, 131 OPS+, .270/.368/.473, 58 XBH (26 HR), 3 SB WAR: 5.1

Over the course of his five-year, $85 million deal with the Cubs, Seiya Suzuki posted a 128 OPS+ and 16.2 WAR while averaging 27 home runs and 92 RBI per 162 games.

His .368 on-base percentage in 2026 was a career high. After he was relegated mostly to DH duty while playing alongside Kyle Tucker in 2025, he put together an excellent season defensively (14 DRS, 5 OAA) and is a finalist for NL Gold Glove honors.

Predicted Contract: 3 years, $66 million

A three-year, $66 million deal would match the contract the Dodgers gave corner outfield slugger Teoscar Hernández when he was the same age, though his status as arguably the No. 2 bat on the market could get him a fourth year.

Age: 28 Stats: 30 GS, 10-11, 4.03 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 157 K, 169.2 IP WAR: 2.2

Trevor Rogers has pitched like a frontline starter at times in his career, including a pristine 1.81 ERA over 109.2 innings during the 2025 season when he finished ninth in AL Cy Young balloting.

His injury history and lackluster 2026 will cap his earning power, but he did toss a career-high 169.2 innings. He finished better than he started, with a 3.52 ERA and 1.05 WHIP in 13 starts after the All-Star break.

Predicted Contract: 4 years, $70 million

The four-year, $68 million deal that Jameson Taillon signed with the Cubs fits the narrative of a talented pitcher who occasionally looked like an ace but often fit better as a No. 3/4 starter.

Age: 29 Stats: 26 GS, 10-10, 3.18 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 159 K, 172.2 IP

Right-hander Hiromi Itoh has a strong track record of production as one of Japan's top starters, posting a 2.91 ERA and 1.17 WHIP in 1,008.2 innings over six seasons with the Nippon-Ham Fighters.

While he lacks the swing-and-miss stuff of some other top arms to come out of the Japanese League with a 21.9 percent career strikeout rate, his age, durability and consistency give him a high floor as a potential No. 3/4 starter stateside.

Predicted Contract: 5 years, $75 million

A five-year, $75 million deal would match the contract Kodai Senga signed when he jumped from Japan to join the Mets. He was also 29 years old at the time.

Age: 30 Stats: 32 GS, 10-11, 4.42 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 156 K, 169.0 IP WAR: 0.7

The Mets paid a steep price to acquire Freddy Peralta from the Brewers last offseason. He took the ball on Opening Day as the ace of the staff. He ended up struggling to a 4.99 ERA and 1.48 WHIP in 113.2 innings and found himself back on the trade block at the deadline.

However, things turned around almost immediately after he joined the Rays. He had a 3.25 ERA and 1.01 WHIP in 55.1 innings to close out the regular season. He has also made two strong playoff starts, including six shutout innings against the Guardians in Game 2 of the ALCS.

Predicted Contract: 4 years, $80 million

The Tigers gave Jack Flaherty a two-year, $35 million deal after an inconsistent season, but he didn't have the same track record as a frontline starter. The four-year, $80 million deal that Eduardo Rodríguez signed with the D-backs feels closer to the market Peralta can expect this winter, with an outside shot at a fifth year.

Age: 27 Stats: 76 G, 28 HLD, 2.83 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 11.2 K/9, 86.0 IP WAR: 1.9

One of the youngest players in the 2026-27 free agent class, Adrian Morejón fits prominently into the conversation of the most dominant left-handed relievers in baseball.

Over the past three seasons, he has posted a 2.58 ERA, 1.09 WHIP and 10.0 K/9 with 60 holds in 211 appearances. His 86.0 innings and 11.2 K/9 in 2026 were both career-high marks. His 107 strikeouts ranked third among all relievers.

Predicted Contract: 5 years, $90 million

The Dodgers gave Tanner Scott a four-year, $72 million deal for a dominant late-inning lefty with swing-and-miss stuff. He was two years older when he hit the open market. A matching AAV and a fifth year seem reasonable for Morejón.

Age: 31 Stats: 670 PA, 148 OPS+, .281/.381/.484, 62 XBH (26 HR), 26 SB WAR: 5.7

Durability and consistency should help Randy Arozarena earn a nine-figure payday, as he has averaged 152 games over the past six seasons while recording at least 20 home runs and 20 steals every year during that span.

His 148 OPS+ in 2026 was a career high and ranked fourth among qualified AL hitters. His .381 on-base percentage was good for fifth on the AL leaderboard. His stellar postseason track record further adds to his appeal for contenders looking for the missing piece offensively.

Predicted Contract: 5 years, $115 million

Nick Castellanos was coming off a career year offensively and was one of the top bats on the market when he signed a five-year, $100 million deal with the Phillies. Arozarena should be able to surpass that contract, despite the fact that he is two years older than Castellanos was when he signed.

Age: 27 Stats: 614 PA, .306/.383/.609, 82 XBH (39 HR), 8 SB

Teruaki Sato won the NPB Triple Crown with the Hanshin Tigers in 2026, hitting .306/39/106. That came on the heels of a 40-homer, 102-RBI campaign the previous year.

With 164 strikeouts and a 26.7 percent strikeout rate, he possesses some of the same swing-and-miss concerns that ultimately limited Munetaka Murakami's market last winter. However, given Murakami's success and Sato's more valuable defensive profile, his earning power might not face the same limitations.

Predicted Contract: 6 years, $120 million

The six-year, $113 million deal that Jung Hoo Lee signed with the Giants looks like a logical starting point for Sato's market. While he is two years older than Lee was when he made the move stateside, the glaring lack of impact bats available this winter should give him a nice boost.

Age: 31 Stats: 32 GS, 12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP WAR: 4.3

Michael King rejoined the Padres last offseason on a three-year, $75 million deal, despite injuries that limited him to just 73.1 innings in 2025. The back-loaded deal included opt-outs after 2026 and 2027. He would be leaving $58 million on the table if he exercises that opt-out.

After a fully healthy season, punctuated by a fantastic postseason (3 G, 2 GS, 1-0, 1 SV, 0.64 ERA, 15 K, 14.0 IP), opting out should be a no-brainer. He would immediately slot in ahead of Trevor Rogers and Freddy Peralta as the No. 2 pitcher on the market.

Predicted Contract: 5 years, $120 million

Robbie Ray signed a five-year, $115 million deal following his Cy Young season in 2021. His earning power was somewhat limited by an inconsistent track record. With only two full seasons as a starter under his belt and injury issues in 2025, King has a comparable free agency outlook.

Age: 29 Stats: 26 GS, 12-7, 2.72 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 186 K, 158.2 IP WAR: 4.6

One of the best starting pitchers to ever hit the free agent market while still being very much in the prime of his career, Tarik Skubal will have his sights on a record-setting contract.

He didn't miss a beat after joining the Dodgers at the deadline, going 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA, 1.05 WHIP and 70 strikeouts in 62 innings. He threw the ball well in a pair of postseason starts.

Predicted Contract: 9 years, $360 million

The nine-year, $324 million deal Gerrit Cole signed with the Yankees at the same age will be the mark Skubal aims to surpass. A $40 million AAV is within reach for the clear headliner of the 2026-27 free-agent class.

articles.title: The 2026 Dodgers and Top 10 Most Expensive MLB Payrolls That Didn't Win the World Series
articles.summary: After winning the World Series in both 2024 and 2025 and winning 100 games this season, it'd be a bit harsh to label the 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers as a failure of epic proportions—even though they did get swept by a Brewers team spending, roughly, one quarter of what the Dodgers spent.
articles.body:
After winning the World Series in both 2024 and 2025 and winning 100 games this season, it'd be a bit harsh to label the 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers as a failure of epic proportions—even though they did get swept by a Brewers team spending, roughly, one quarter of what the Dodgers spent.

It is, however, the ultimate failure of epic payroll.

Their estimated competitive balance tax payroll of $433.1M is the highest in MLB history, and therefore also the most money ever spent by a team that didn't win a World Series.

But how does the rest of the top 10 stack up?

What we did account for : Inflation. According to the inflation calculator on the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics website, $1 in July 2000 equates to $1.95 today, $1 in July 2005 equates to $1.72 today and so on and so forth. Got to adjust for inflation in a discussion like this.

What we didn't account for : Deferred salaries or competitive balance tax payments. The 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers are going to pay an estimated luxury tax of more than $180M, but they've also deferred something like $150M of their 2026 payroll, so it kind of comes out in the wash? We're ignoring all that, though, and focusing strictly on the year-end competitive balance tax payrolls.*

*Back to 2012, at least. From 2000-11, Cot's Contracts only provides a year-end 40-man payroll captured by the Associated Press. But the year-end 40-man payroll and CB payroll totals are generally in the same ballpark.

Without further ado, avert your eyes, Dodgers and Mets fans.

Recent High Spenders Spared by the Inflation Factor

If we hadn't bothered to account for inflation, we could've just stopped the research at 2023. Prior to that, no team had ever had a $300M payroll, but there have been 13 north of that threshold since.

As such, there are quite a few recent big spenders who didn't crack our top 10. But let's at least mention them here.

2026 Toronto Blue Jays ($315.8M, no inflation adjustment)

The Blue Jays got close to $300M during their run to the World Series in 2025. But between Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s extension and signing Dylan Cease, Kazuma Okamoto and more this past winter, they blew right by that mark for the first time. A lot of good that did them, though, going 79-83 with the lowest-scoring offense in the majors.

2025 Philadelphia Phillies ($314.3M, $330M with inflation) 2026 Philadelphia Phillies ($322.2M, no inflation adjustment)

The Phillies have ranked fourth in payroll in each of the past six seasons. But the concern at this point is how much money they already have tied up in aging veterans for the next six or so years. They have at least made the postseason in each of the last five seasons, but with no World Series rings to show for it.

2024 New York Yankees ($316.2M, $338M with inflation) 2025 New York Yankees ($319.5M, $335M with inflation) 2026 New York Yankees ($341.9M, no inflation adjustment)

Fear not. The Yankees will make a couple of appearances in the top 10. But as fans of this team know all too well, it's been a while since the days when they were aggressively outspending everyone on an annual basis.

The Yankees did make it to the World Series in 2024, but got knocked out in the ALDS by the AL East champion in each of the past two years.

Who would've guessed when Luis Gonzalez walked it off against Mariano Rivera in 2001 that the Yankees would win just one of the next 25 World Series?

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $285.6M

The 2021 NLDS between the 106-win Dodgers and 107-win Giants was an all-timer of a clash of the two best teams during the regular season. But after surviving that five-game battle, the Dodgers fell to the 88-win Atlanta Braves in the NLCS, when what had been a fantastic starting rotation during the regular season simply could not cut the mustard against... *checks notes* ...Eddie Rosario.

Bauer only pitched for the first three months of his three-year, $102 million Dodgers contract before being placed on administrative leave. He was later suspended and never pitched for the team again. On the mound, however, he delivered strong results: 14 quality starts in 17 appearances, a 2.59 ERA and 11.5 K/9.

Biggest Waste of Funds : Cody Bellinger ($16.1M)

This is where the 2017 NL Rookie of the Year and 2019 NL MVP really bottomed out. Bellinger underwent shoulder surgery in November 2020 and then suffered a broken leg less than a week into the 2021 regular season. He hit a brutal .165 during the regular season, but did at least show up with a .906 OPS in the postseason.

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $218.3M Adjusted for Inflation : $355.8M Record : 94-68

Remember Joba Chamberlain's infamous midges game in Cleveland? That was Game 2 of this ALDS, when the flamethrowing rookie was eaten alive by bugs in the eighth inning, leading to two walks, two wild pitches and a hit batter while blowing the lead. As a result, the Yankees returned home in a 2-0 hole and were unable to climb out of it.

From an OPS perspective (1.067), 2007 was the greatest season of A-Rod's career. He led the majors with 54 home runs and 156 RBI and also stole 24 bases en route to winning his third AL MVP almost unanimously. His subsequent 10-year, $275M contract did not age well for New York, but he was incredible the year before temporarily hitting free agency.

Biggest Waste of Funds : Jason Giambi ($23.4M)

During Giambi's 7-year, $120M contract with the Yankees, he had at least 32 home runs and an OPS north of .875 five times. This was...not one of those years. Plantar fasciitis sidelined him for a good chunk of the 2007 season, and he was nowhere near his usual self when he did play. He ended up making just four plate appearances during the '07 ALDS against Cleveland.

Brewers have Dodgers' dynasty on life support

Ranking Top 25 Trade Chips For Offseason 🔢

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $207.2M Adjusted for Inflation : $358.4M Record : 95-67

Once upon a time, the Angels were a regular in the postseason. And in the 2005 ALDS, Bengie Molina brought the lumber for home runs in Games 1, 2 and 3. In the do-or-die Game 5, however, it was Adam Kennedy playing hero with a two-run triple off Mike Mussina before Francisco 'K-Rod' Rodríguez closed out the series.

As was the case with the 2007 iteration we just encountered, giving A-Rod a ton of money in 2005 was a pretty good idea for the Yankees—at least during the regular season. This, too, was one of his MVP campaigns, batting .321/.421/.610 with 48 home runs, 130 RBI and 21 stolen bases. (He was a ghost in the ALDS, though, going 2-for-15 with no RBI.)

Biggest Waste of Funds : Kevin Brown ($15.7M)

At 40 years old, Brown was in the final season of a 7-year, $105M deal, as well as the final season of his career. And in 13 appearances, he gave the Yankees a 6.50 ERA, last appearing in a game that July.

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $359.5M Adjusted for Inflation : $359.5M Record : 74-88

New York's season was over seemingly before it started. The Mets went 7-19 in April and never even remotely flirted with getting back to .500—a path made more maddening by the fact that Boston, Houston and Philadelphia were just as terrible early on before all rallying to make the playoffs.

Soto missed 51 games between his two stints on the IL, but he was one of New York's only particularly productive hitters while healthy. Soto hit 27 home runs en route to his 154 OPS+. And had he logged enough plate appearances to qualify, his .393 on-base percentage would have led the National League.

Biggest Waste of Funds : Bo Bichette ($42M)

For better or worse, Bichette did play in almost every game for the Mets. But in the first season of that gargantuan three-year, $126M contract, he barely managed a .700 OPS and wasn't exactly a great glove at the hot corner. It's hard to believe he's considering opting out of the other two years after that dud of a season.

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $346.7M Adjusted for Inflation : $364.0M Record : 83-79

On the final day of the regular season, the New York Mets were shut out 4-0 by a sub-.500 Miami Marlins team playing for nothing but pride. As a result, the Mets missed out on the postseason on a tiebreaker with the Cincinnati Reds, getting an early start on an offseason that was allegedly designed to improve their run prevention in 2026.

Soto started slow in the first season of his 15-year, $765M contract, batting .224 into late May. But over his final 105 games, he sure looked like an MVP, racking up 35 home runs and 31 stolen bases with a 1.014 OPS. He ended up two swipes shy of the 40/40 club.

Biggest Waste of Funds : Sean Manaea ($22M)

The ace of New York's staff in 2024, Manaea was a mess in the first year of his newly minted contract. He didn't make his season debut until the final game before the All-Star Break, and he never managed to tally a single quality start amid his 5.64 ERA. And in starting the aforementioned must-win Game 162, he didn't even make it out of the second inning.

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $347.7M Adjusted for Inflation : $372.0M Record : 89-73

After making the postseason as part of a three-way tie for the last two spots, the Mets caught fire, eliminating both the Brewers and Phillies on their way to a star-studded NLCS against the Dodgers. But this Mets pitching staff had no answer for a Los Angeles offense that averaged 7.7 runs in the series, culminating in a 10-5 elimination game.

Lindor has had a lot of high-quality seasons throughout his career, but this was the closest he has come to winning an MVP. In the end, there was no debate, with Shohei Ohtani winning unanimously. But with 33 home runs, 29 stolen bases and excellent defense at shortstop, Lindor was the first runner-up.

Biggest Waste of Funds : Max Scherzer ($30.8M)

This was the money the Mets retained when they traded away Mad Max the previous summer. (They also retained $25M of Justin Verlander's 2024 salary.) For Scherzer, they got Luisangel Acuña. He gave them very little for 1.5 seasons before they traded him for Luis Robert Jr., which also did not age well.

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $277.7M

The 2014 NLDS is when Clayton Kershaw's postseason struggles first became a full-blown narrative. After he put together one of the best regular seasons ever, winning both the NL Cy Young and NL MVP awards, the Cardinals tattooed him for eight earned runs in Game 1. He was better in Game 4, but also took the L in that series finale.

Greinke had quite the run through the mid-2010s, winning 51 games in the span of three seasons with a 2.30 ERA. This year was the midpoint of that stretch, giving the Dodgers more than 200 innings pitched and more than 200 strikeouts. He also gave them something that Kershaw couldn't: a postseason gem. In LA's only win of the 2014 postseason, Greinke went seven scoreless innings.

Biggest Waste of Funds : Andre Ethier ($17M)

Through the first eight seasons of his career, Ethier triple-slashed .288/.362/.470, averaging 18 home runs per season. But he spontaneously combusted in 2014, posting a .691 OPS while homering just four times. Over the final two months of the season, he was little more than an expensive pinch hitter.

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $374.7M

The 2026 Dodgers are No. 1 on the list with a payroll about $17M higher, but this was the most emphatic expensive failure of all time. The Mets sputtered through the first two months before absolutely imploding in June to the tune of a 7-19 record. They then spent the week leading up to the trade deadline trying to salvage anything they could from this sinking ship.

Top Earner : Justin Verlander and Max Scherzer ($43.3M apiece)

Year No. 1 with Scherzer making $43.3M went so well in 2022 that the Mets doubled down on reuniting him with Verlander in 2023. That pair of old timers wasn't quite what New York was hoping for, but they also weren't terrible by any means. Each had a winning record and a bWAR north of 2.0 before the Mets traded both of them away.

Biggest Waste of Funds : Edwin Díaz ($20.4M)

The Mets signed Díaz to a record-setting 5-year, $102M contract in November 2022, but that freak injury in the World Baseball Classic kept him from throwing a single pitch for them in 2023. As it turned out, though, there weren't too many late leads to protect anyway.

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $297.9M Adjusted for Inflation : $423.0M Record : 92-70

The 2015 Dodgers spent nearly 25 percent more than the second-priciest roster that season, but even that couldn't buy them a postseason series victory. They ran into Jacob deGrom and the New York Mets in the NLDS. He mowed them down with a combined 20 strikeouts in winning Games 1 and 5. And in the one game New York won that deGrom didn't start, the Mets went off for 13 runs in Game 3.

Though not quite as dominant as he was in 2014, Kershaw also had a phenomenal run through 2015. He led the majors in innings pitched (232.2), total strikeouts (301) and FIP (1.99). And that was after a rocky start to the year. He had a ludicrous 1.39 ERA over his final 24 starts.

Biggest Waste of Funds : Carl Crawford ($20.3M)

No season of Crawford's 7-year, $142M contract was particularly good, but this was the year that things really went off the rails. He missed nearly three months of action with a torn oblique muscle and had to battle for playing time upon his return in late July. He went 1-for-12 in the NLDS.

Competitive Balance Tax Payroll : $433.1M Adjusted for Inflation : $433.1M Record : 100-62

In sweeping the Milwaukee Brewers out of the 2025 NLCS, the Dodgers held that foe to just one home run. That shoe was on the other foot in this NLCS, though, with Shohei Ohtani providing Los Angeles' only four-bagger of the series while Milwaukee clubbed seven of them. The 103-win Brewers were the better team pretty much all season long, but nobody saw this thumping coming.

Technically, Ohtani has a $46.1M luxury tax salary. But it's a 10-year, $700M contract that the Dodgers are mostly paying later, and it's the contract that first made the Dodgers public enemy No. 1 for 29 of the 30 fanbases. Ohtani's season was going remarkably well (even by his standards) until the knee and biceps injuries that derailed his pitching in early July and his hitting about a month later. He still ended up leading the team in bWAR , though.

Biggest Waste of Funds : Kyle Tucker ($60M)

To his credit, Tucker did eventually show up in a big way. He had a 1.072 OPS over his final 17 regular season games before batting .333 with three extra-base hits in the postseason. But until he flipped that switch in early September, this 4-year, $240M contract was rapidly trending in the direction of Anthony Rendon and Stephen Strasburg's 7-year, $245M nightmares, posting a .671 OPS through his first 137 games with the Dodgers.

articles.title: Dodgers' Miguel Rojas Retires from MLB After Sweep vs. Brewers, Won 2 World Series
articles.summary: The end of the Los Angeles Dodgers' season also marked the end of Miguel Rojas' 13-year MLB career.
articles.body:
The end of the Los Angeles Dodgers' season also marked the end of Miguel Rojas' 13-year MLB career.

Rojas told reporters after the Dodgers' Game 4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLCS on Thursday night that he was retiring.

"This is it, guys. This is it," Rojas said. "I'm gonna move on and go to the next step of my life, in my career, and the baseball world. Today was the last time that I wore that uniform as a player and my cleats. It's really hard to take them off right now."

Brewers have Dodgers' dynasty on life support

Rojas originally entered pro ball in 2006 when he was signed as an international free agent by the Cincinnati Reds. He never reached the big leagues with the club, became a free agent after 2012 and signed with the Dodgers.

After spending another year in the minors, Rojas finally received a call up in June 2014 and he appeared in 85 games with Los Angeles.

The Dodgers traded Rojas to the Miami Marlins in December 2014. He would spend eight seasons with the Marlins, appearing in 870 games during that period from 2015 to '22.

Rojas was traded back to the Dodgers in January 2023 where he would spend the final four years of his career. He had the best year of his career in 2024 with a .283/.337/.410 slash line to help Los Angeles win the first of its two straight World Series titles.

The 2025 World Series featured the peak moment of Rojas' career. He hit the game-tying home run in the top of the ninth inning in Game 7 against the Toronto Blue Jays. Los Angeles went on to win 5-4 in 11 innings.

Rojas had 57 home runs in his entire career up to that point. It was only the second game in the series against the Blue Jays that he started after coming off the bench in the first five games.

The 37-year-old Rojas will end his career with a .260/.313/.363 slash line in 1,401 games played and two World Series championships.

articles.title: What is your best-case scenario for the Phillies offseason?
articles.summary: Getting into a positive mindset for the weekend
articles.body:
Yesterday, our topic of discussion was what is your own worst-case scenario for what the Phillies will do this offseason. Today, we're going to try and envision a scenario where everything goes right, or at least as right as possible.

Like we mentioned yesterday, the Phillies have their work cut out for them. The free agent market is weak, but the Phillies should have plenty of money to use on it to find whatever upgrades are possible. They will be freeing up close to $40M in dead money with the contracts of Nick Castellanos and Taijuan Walker alone coming off the books. Add in the likely subtraction of José Alvarado's $12M and Alec Bohm's $10M salaries, and the Phillies will likely be around $50M under their 2026 payroll commitments after arbitration. Through all of their faults, the team has yet to waver on its commitment to operating with a payroll around the top five highest in MLB. Until they signal that is no longer the case, you should feel some confidence that they will spend somewhere around or at least equal to the $290M they featured at this season's end.

The Phillies desperately need upgrades and some new life, but they also have a good core to work with. Cristopher Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo are both ace level starters that are locked up long term. Zack Wheeler is still under contract for one final season. Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, no matter what you may think of their peak abilities at this stage of their careers, were still top 15 hitters in MLB by OPS this season. The rest of the lineup needs major improvements, but those two are two very good starting points. The bullpen was a mess, but Jhoan Duran was one of the best closers in baseball, and he is still under contract through 2028. You can debate what that group's ceiling is, but they have a very high floor, provided of course there are no devastating injuries which are admittedly a risk with some of the ages involved. A perfect offseason would involve finding the right additions to raise that floor.

Finally, perhaps the biggest reason for optimism heading into next season is the resurgence of Andrew Painter. the young right hander returned from a demotion to Triple-A in late July and looked like a new pitcher, capping off his season with a tremendous showing out of the bullpen in the postseason. Perhaps Painter isn't capable of becoming the pitcher he was pre-Tommy John surgery, but he showed enough last season to have one hopeful that he can still be a good piece for the future.

So, what is your best-case scenario for the Phillies this offseason? What free agents would satisfy you? Any particular trades that you're set on?

articles.summary: Major League Baseball will soon crown a new World Series champion.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball will soon crown a new World Series champion.

The Milwaukee Brewers, fresh off their NLCS sweep of the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers, have booked their second ever World Series trip and are four wins away from capturing the franchise's first title. The ALCS, meanwhile, features a Tampa Bay Rays team similarly pursuing its first championship, and a Cleveland Guardians club aiming to end a 78-year championship drought.

Regardless how things play out from here, one fan base will soon be rewarded with a memory of a lifetime. Of course, two other fan bases will be crushed with colossal disappointment, but hey, that's baseball.

Game 1: ALCS winner at Milwaukee Brewers (Fox)

Game 2: ALCS winner at Milwaukee Brewers (Fox)

Game 3: Milwaukee Brewers at ALCS winner on Fox

Game 4: Milwaukee Brewers at ALCS winner on Fox

Game 5: Milwaukee Brewers at ALCS winner on Fox*

Game 6: ALCS winner at Milwaukee Brewers (Fox)*

Game 7: ALCS winner at Milwaukee Brewers (Fox)*

With only half of the World Series bracket set, a projected ALCS winner must be crowned before advancing to the championship round. And despite Cleveland's 3-2 triumph in Thursday's Game 3, our crystal ball still sees Tampa prevailing (though a Guardians' win in Game 4 would flip that).

Seeing Tampa and Milwaukee in the final round should be a dream outcome for any baseball fans. Broadcasters might covet bigger markets and more established stars, but this would pit the top seeds in each league going head-to-head for the throne.

It would also pit two near mirror-image teams against one another. Both the Brewers and Rays are masterful payroll-maximizers, squeezing everything they can from their rosters with a blend of contact hitting, baserunning, timely power, elite defense and lockdown bullpens.

Oddsmakers might call a Brewers-Rays championship clash a coin flip, and honestly, that's close to how we'd view it, too. But Milwaukee has some notable edges, like homefield advantage, additional rest (Tampa is, at minimum, three games away from the final round) and the league's most dynamic starter in Jacob Misiorowski, who's up to 263 strikeouts in 182 innings (playoffs included).

articles.title: Brewers Honor Former Players With NLCS Champagne Bottles in New Photos from World Series Celebration
articles.summary: After clinching a berth in the World Series for the first time in 44 years on Thursday night, the Milwaukee Brewers used their postgame celebration to honor players from the franchise's past.
articles.body:
After clinching a berth in the World Series for the first time in 44 years on Thursday night, the Milwaukee Brewers used their postgame celebration to honor players from the franchise's past.

Photos from inside the Brewers' locker room showed they had champagne bottles with labels featuring player names and the years they made the postseason with the club.

Some of the names featured include Baseball Hall of Famer Rollie Fingers, Rowdy Tellez, Jeff Suppan, Curtis Granderson and Jace Peterson.

The Brewers also had champagne bottles with the names of various towns in Wisconsin, similar to the flag the team has carried around throughout this playoff run.

One year after being swept by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS, the Brewers returned the favor. They capped off their four-game sweep with a 6-4 victory in Dodger Stadium to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982.

The Brewers will host Game 1 of the World Series on Oct. 23. They await the winner of the ALCS between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays.

articles.title: World Series hero Miguel Rojas emotionally announces retirement after Dodgers get swept in NLCS
articles.summary: Miguel Rojas announced his retirement after the Los Angeles Dodgers' sweep loss to Milwaukee Brewers, ending a 13-year career that included a legendary World Series moment.
articles.body: Los Angeles Dodgers World Series hero Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from baseball Thursday at age 37. After the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Dodgers 6-4 to complete the sweep and advance to the World Series, an emotional Rojas said he was hanging up his spikes. "No, I think this is it, guys," Rojas told reporters postgame. "This is it as a player. That was my last game played. That was the last time that I put these cleats on and this uniform on as a player. From now on, I'm going to start thinking about what's going to happen in my life as a baseball person." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Rojas was responsible for one of the biggest swings in Dodgers history. articles.body: We saw the end of a dynasty on Thursday night. I suppose if you're a Los Angeles Dodgers hater, you're happy. If you're a fan of the "small market" club, then you're happy as well. Baseball is one of those things where it almost doesn't matter who you have on the team. Just like in hockey, whichever team hits wins the game. We are now assured of two teams being in the bottom half of the league in payroll, representing the league in the World Series. The Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians play Game 3 on Friday night. The Rays came into this series as the best team in the American League. Their regular season saw them win 98 games and take the top spot in the League. They swept the New York Yankees in the ALDS and didn't even really sweat in that series. Now they are down 2-1 after having the lead in all three games. It is hard to close out games in the playoffs, but the Guardians seem to have the same never-say-die mentality that the Milwaukee Brewers have. Their hitting really hasn't been bad, and their pitching has been strong, but the Guardians have just been a bit better in both areas. Tonight, the Rays send out Nick Martinez to the hill. In the regular season, Martinez went 15-6 with a 3.10 ERA and a 1.09 WHIP. Those numbers were all top-15 in baseball. He made the first road start of the ALDS against New York, and he allowed two earned runs over 3.2 innings on five hits. The good news for Tampa fans is that Martinez has been elite against the Guardians this season. He has two starts this year against Cleveland, and he allowed seven hits and no walks in 13 scoreless innings this season. Jose Ramirez is 1-for-11 against him. He has only seen one out of work for the postseason. It was in the 9-5 Guardians win over the Chicago White Sox, and he allowed two earned runs and two walks. articles.title: The Dodgers' Growing Problem With Shohei Ohtani
articles.summary: In Year 3 of what is meant to be a 10-year partnership, the Los Angeles Dodgers need to decide what to do with Shohei Ohtani.
articles.body:
In Year 3 of what is meant to be a 10-year partnership, the Los Angeles Dodgers need to decide what to do with Shohei Ohtani.

There was nothing to it in 2024 and 2025. "Just let him cook" was the vibe coming out of Chavez Ravine, and no one could argue with the results. A 50-50 season in one year. A 55-homer season, with elite pitching on the side. A World Series championship and an MVP award for both.

It therefore borders on the brain-breaking to behold the wreckage of 2026. There are the smoldering ruins of the Dodgers after a four-game sweep by the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLCS. And there is Ohtani, who was too hurt to do much of anything in the last two months of the season.

What happens next is hard to tell. It depends on who learned what, and how strongly. Hard questions must be asked, and there won't be answers until someone blinks.

The Dodgers and Shohei Ohtani Both Own the Failures of 2026

The "Just let him cook" model worked just fine for Ohtani and the Dodgers for most of this season. He went into the All-Star break with a .953 OPS and 22 home runs as a hitter and a 1.79 ERA in 14 starts as a pitcher. He had one hand on his fifth MVP, which would have pushed him into territory previously known only to Barry Bonds.

Even then, though, there were quiet whispers of a physical breakdown that would gradually grow into a dull roar.

First, it was just his left knee . Then, it was his right biceps . The pitching stopped for good on July 3. The hitting stopped on August 18, at least based on the results. He had a .949 OPS and 30 homers on the day. After that, a .530 OPS and no homers. Even after Ohtani finally got off the long ball schneid in NLCS Game 4, he still exited the postseason with only a .630 OPS and one homer.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts may have intentionally lit the fire that sent that homer soaring into the LA night. He had floated benching Ohtani for Game 3, and then implied during Game 4 that Ohtani had been motivated by the resulting chatter. If so, Roberts clearly understands how to get through to his famously non-communicative superstar.

However, accusations of mismanagement by Roberts and the Dodgers are backed by too much evidence. It wasn't until September 11 that the Dodgers finally placed Ohtani on the IL, where he stayed for two weeks. He still wasn't fully healthy when the playoffs began, and he never looked it during the Dodgers' briefer-than-expected stay. He struck out 14 times in 30 at-bats, at times looking like he had never swung a bat before .

According to Katie Woo of The Athletic , Ohtani said Thursday that it's "hard to tell" whether he'll need surgery for his injuries. That is notably not an outright rejection of the possibility, and that should make the Dodgers cringe.

It fuels the notion that Ohtani was too hurt to be playing all along. And with the upcoming lockout shutting down player-team communication , the last thing they need this offseason is their $700 million unicorn recovering from surgery in a black box known only to him and his equally secretive agent , Nez Balelo.

The Dodgers and Shohei Ohtani Need to Find a Happy Medium

Whatever happens with Ohtani during the offseason, now is the perfect time to discuss whether his two-way player act has finally become too much for him to bear.

He is 32 years old, after all, and he's already had two major surgeries on his right arm. Since it serves as both his landing leg when pitching and his back leg when hitting, it can't be emphasized strongly enough just how much Ohtani can't move forward with a compromised left knee.

And yet, he has already determined that there is no conversation to be had.

"Yes, definitely," Ohtani said when asked if he remained committed to pitching, according to Woo. He also added that he is "looking forward to having a better season next year."

Even if the Dodgers aren't ready to fight this, they must be ready to push back on letting Ohtani run his own show amid what should be a 26-man circus. And they just might be, if earlier quotes (presented by Woo) from Roberts and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman are any indication:

Dave Roberts: "It's different than any player, you might argue, in any sport right now because he's a global phenomenon. Certainly it's tougher to manage, and I've got to be mindful."

Andrew Friedman: "What he's doing is unprecedented, and it takes a real toll. It's unprecedented for all of us, and we're kind of feeling our way through it together."

If the Dodgers can't convince Ohtani to stop pitching, their options for managing his workload are ultimately limited. He's already on a once-per-week schedule, with all but one of his 14 starts this year coming on six days of rest or more.

The only logical step is for the Dodgers to declare that Ohtani can't have it both ways on the same day.

He might not like it, but there's decent evidence that it would be for the best. In games where he hits but doesn't pitch, he has a career OPS of .951. In games where he does both, he has a .897 OPS. While his pitching excellence is arguably worth the modest drop-off in his offense, that argument falls apart if the risk of injury grows. After 2026, the Dodgers simply must treat that as the truth.

Somehow, some way, the Dodgers and Ohtani need to figure this out. Because barring a scenario in which Dodgers owner Mark Walter quickly sells the team and allows Ohtani to trigger an unusual opt-out clause , the two sides still have seven years left together.

They can, and should, be seven great years, but only if 2026 is treated as a warning rather than a one-off.

articles.title: Tarik Skubal Reacts to Dodgers' MLB Playoff Exit in Video After NLCS Sweep, 'So Hard to Win'
articles.summary: Tarik Skubal didn't want to talk about his impending free agency following the Los Angeles Dodgers' season-ending loss on Thursday night, but he did address the difficulty of winning at the highest level.
articles.body:
Tarik Skubal didn't want to talk about his impending free agency following the Los Angeles Dodgers' season-ending loss on Thursday night, but he did address the difficulty of winning at the highest level.

After the Dodgers were swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLCS, Skubal told reporters it's "so hard to win" when asked about winning in the playoffs.

"It's extremely difficult," Skubal said. "There's a lot of really good teams, a lot really talented players across the league. It's so hard to win. Seeing what the Dodgers have done the last two years, you think it's easy, but it's really not."

The Dodgers were swept in a best-of-seven playoff series for the first time since the 1966 World Series. They led at one point in all four games against the Brewers, but the late innings were a key difference between the two teams.

Milwaukee outscored the Dodgers 10-2 between innings six through nine. Another issue in the series was Los Angeles couldn't buy a hit with a runner in scoring position, going 4-of-27 in those situations.

Thursday's loss felt particularly crushing, beyond ending their season, because the Dodgers actually got a highlight moment from Shohei Ohtani. He hit a three-run homer in the bottom of the second that gave Los Angeles a 4-0 lead. It was his first home run since Aug. 18.

Those were the last runs the Dodgers scored in the game. Milwaukee scored six unanswered runs to clinch its first World Series appearance since 1982.

Skubal did his part to help the team in their quest for a third straight World Series title. He allowed three runs on seven hits with 14 strikeouts in 11 innings over two playoff starts.

The Dodgers' loss means the 1998-2000 New York Yankees remain the last MLB team to win three consecutive World Series championships.

articles.title: The Season That Was: Kevin Gausman
articles.summary: A look at Kevin Gausman’s 2026 season
articles.body:
2026 was the final season of Kevin Gausman's five-year, $110 million free-agent contract. In the first four seasons, Kevin posted a 48-41 record, a 3.48 ERA, and an 11.5 bWAR. A good return on a big free-agent contract. Not all that many of those go as well as this one did.

But 2026 was his age-35 season, and sometimes pitchers don't do well in their mid-30s.

Provided by Baseball-Reference.com : View Original Table Generated 10/15/2026.

Baseball Reference has him at a 1.1 WAR (down from 4.0). FanGraphs 3.1 (down from 4.1), giving him a value of $25.1 million to the Jays and Cubs.

He had a 3.3.74 FIP and a 3.58 xFIP, which is why the FanGraphs WAR is so much better than the Baseball Reference one.

Kevin's BABIP was .311 (up from.262 last year). 68.7% of his base runner were stranded (down from 72.2%).

His line drive rate was down a little bit (19.6% from 21.3 last year), ground ball rate up (40.3% down from 36.7), and fly ball rate much the same (40.3% from 42.0). 12.7% of fly balls hit off him left the park, up from 9.5.

His strikeout rate about the same (24.5% from 24.4), and his walk rate was down a bit (6.3% from 6.5).

Kevin's soft contact was up (17.4% from 15.1 last year) and hard contact about the same (35.9% from 36.2).

He was better against LHB (.251/.304/.389) than RHB (.269/.307/.459). He's been slightly better against LHB for his career.

He was better at home (3.83 ERA, batters hit .264/.299/.439) than on the road (5.40, .253/.313/.394).

Kevin was better in the first half of the season (4.33, .244/.296/.405) than the second half (4.82, .284/.320/.444).

April: 7 starts, 2-2, 3.10. Batters hit .204/.244/.349, 5 home runs, 8 walks and 40 strikeouts.

May: 5 starts, 2-1, 3.18. Batters hit .291/.316/.364, 1 home run, 4 walks and 26 strikeouts.

June: 6 starts, 0-4, 6.47. Batters hit .262/.324/.556, 9 home runs, 12 walks and 34 strikeouts.

July: 4 starts, 0-3, 6.10. Batters hit .280/.366/.317, 3 home runs, 11 walks and 23 strikeouts.

August: 6 starts, 4-1, 4.54. Batters hit .275/.312/.443, 5 home runs, 8 walks and 33 strikeouts.

September: 4 starts, 1-1, 4.43. Batters hit .267/.298/.478, 6 home runs, 4 walks and 28 strikeouts.

The Jays were 9-14 in his starts. The Cubs were 5-4 in his starts. Between the two teams, they averaged 4.05 runs scored in games he started. They scored 2 or less runs in 13 of his starts.

6 or more days, 4 games: 4.50, .275/.326/.413

I love guys who are best on normal rest. I think we are all creatures of habit, you get in a routine and things go well, you leave that routine and they don't got as well. He was also best on normal rest last year.

And he faced 1 batter a fourth time, getting the out.

I wonder if he would consider being a reliever next year? That might be reading too much into one season, in 2025 he was pretty much the same for each of the first three times through the order.

Brandon Valenzuela: 4.46, .254/.298/.396 in 308 PA.

Alejandro Kirk: 4.81, .263/.324/.419 in 185 PA.

Carson Kelly: 4.20, .226/.268/.426 in 123 PA.

Miguel Amaya: 5.75, .305/.333/.500 in 87 PA.

Tyler Heineman: 2.31, .273/.319/.409 in 47 PA.

Kevin's best start, by GameScore, was a 78 on April 1st, at home against the Rockies. He went 6 innings, 2 hits, 0 earned runs, 0 walks, and 10 strikeouts. He also had a 77 and two 76s.

Worst start? A 13 in Chicago against the Cubs, on June 19th. You likely remember it: 2 innings, 7 hits, 7 earned runs, 1 home run, 4 walks and 3 strikeouts. We used six relievers, two days after a bullpen day, and the next day Patrick Corbin was pulled after 3.2 innings.

Kevin averaged 5.5 innings per start in his 23 starts with us. And about the same in his 9 starts with the Cubs. His one playoff start didn't go all that well: 3.1 innings, 3 earned.

He threw, for the most part, three pitches:

Four Seamer: 93.8 mph (last year it averaged 94.5). Batters hit .289 against it (.230 last year).

Split finger: 84 mph (last year it averaged 94.9). Batters hit .207 against it (.191 last year).

Slider: 84.1 mph (last year it averaged 83.2). Batters hit .324 against it (.333 last year).

Breaking Ball Run Value: 7th percentile.

With the Jays, he posted a 53-51 record and a 3.63 ERA, with a 12.5 bWAR (and a 21 fWAR). FanGraphs says he was worth $167.6 million over his five-year contract, and he was paid $110 million, so we got more than our money's worth.

11th in wins: 53 (tied with Jose Berrios)

He also started 7 playoff games (and pitched once in relief) for the Jays. He had a 3.79 ERA and a 2-4 record.

The last I saw, Gausman was talking about retirement, but he has said that he would consider coming back to the Jays. As I mentioned above, he was terrific the first time through the order, and far less good the second and third times. But I'm not sure that he would want to come back to pitch out of the pen.

The trade looks very good for the Jays, Brett Bateman was terrific for us, in his 41 games. Ty Southisene played well for 11 games with Vancouver, hitting .262/.380/.429. It will be interesting to watch how he does. FanGraphs had him listed as the Cubs 27th best prospect. He's fast and plays good defense in the middle of the infield.

It was great getting to watch Gausman pitch. The last five seasons wouldn't have been nearly as much fun without him.

articles.title: Ranking the Rockies, 2026: No. 41, Zac Veen
articles.summary: The 2020 first-round pick transformed himself in the offseason and tore through Triple-A, but struggled at the MLB level
articles.body:
Welcome to the 2026 edition of Ranking the Rockies, where we take a look back at every player to log playing time for the Rockies in 2026. The purpose of this list is to provide a snapshot of the player in context. The "Ranking" is an organizing principle that's drawn from Baseball Reference's WAR (rWAR). It's not something the staff debated. We'll begin with the player with the lowest rWAR and end up with the player with the highest.

Zac Veen ( No. 6 PuRP ) has had a lot of ups and downs in his tenure with the Rockies.

There was a lot of excitement when the outfielder was drafted ninth overall in 2020 out of Spruce Creek High School in Port Orange, FL and he ended up making his MLB debut on April 8, 2025 after nearly breaking camp with the team.

Veen played 12 games with the Rockies in 2025, slashing just .118/.189/.235 with eight total bases and 14 strikeouts. He fared a little better in Triple-A Albuquerque — slashing .289/.354/.468 through 90 games — but it was revealed in spring training 2026 that Veen was dealing with substance abuse off the field.

When he arrived at Salt River Fields to start 2026, Veen was a different player.

He'd put on about 43 pounds from the end of last season, and was a new player both physically and mentally. Veen played in 11 spring games, hitting .250/.375/.550 with two homers.

He was optioned to Albuquerque to start the year, and absolutely tore through the Pacific Coast League. Ahead of his call-up on August 11th , Veen was hitting a scorching .327/.402/.635 with 24 home runs and 18 stolen bases. He was named PCL Player of the Month for June — where he hit .366/.385/.782 with 24 extra-base hits — as well as back-to-back PCL Player of the Week for the weeks of August 2nd and August 9th .

Veen was recalled on August 11th and made his MLB re-debut on August 12th against the Arizona Diamondbacks. He immediately made his presence known by hitting a home run into the pool at Chase Field in his first game back:

He doubled down by hitting a splash home run into McCovey Cove in San Francisco in the very next game:

He also had that wild play at home on August 16th:

Veen came back with a vengeance, but it didn't last.

After about a week, he began to cool off both at the plate and in the field. He was primarily used as a late-inning pinch hitter, or he would be pinch-hit for late in games. He didn't make much of a case for himself, though, as he also committed numerous blunders in the field (though only two were scored as errors).

The most egregious ones were on September 17th against the San Diego Padres, where Jackson Merrill and Xander Bogaerts hit back-to-back triples, though they could've been scored as errors.

He also bobbled a few during the season-closing Diamondbacks series.

As shown by his -4 OAA and -5 DRS, Veen's defense left much to be desired, especially late in the season.

Offensively, Veen slashed just .232/.312/.435 in 36 games. It's not a terrible line, but it's nothing to write home about either. The 39.2% strikeout rate is, though, as it was second only to Braxton Fulford (40.0%) and nearly double his strikeout rate in Albuquerque (20.4%).

Skyler Timmins wrote about Veen's performance in early September, and not much has changed since then.

Veen's torrid Triple-A season was rewarded, though, as he finished the year as Baseball America's Triple-A Player of the Year , PCL MVP — the first Rockies prospect to win the award since Nolan Arenado's cousin Joshua Fuentes in 2018 — and a postseason All-Star.

As the Rockies continue their rebuild, there will be some tough decisions to make.

articles.title: These Brewers aren't Cinderella. They might be MLB's next behemoth
articles.summary: Milwaukee's climb to the NL pennant has been slow and methodical over the past decade. In the process, the Brewers have become one of the best organizations...
articles.body:
A dejected Matt Arnold, president of baseball operations for the Milwaukee Brewers, walked into an elevator at Dodger Stadium following Game 4 of the 2025 NLCS with an ashen face. It was as if he'd just watched a horror movie. And for the organization trying to get over a then-43-year hump and its fan base, they had. With the Brewers being swept in embarrassing fashion by the eventual World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers, the reality that they had not yet arrived was setting in.

One year later, the Brewers watched a different movie, a feel-good flick, unfold. This time, Milwaukee was the victor. Not only are the Brewers heading to the World Series for the first time since 1982 , but they also got there by dominating those same Dodgers who were boogeymen last fall. In the process, the Brewers have ended MLB's third-longest World Series appearance drought .

"The series prior to playing the Dodgers last year took a lot out of us. I think Murph has talked about that a lot," Arnold said of manager Pat Murphy last week. "Same thing with the Padres. That's just part of it. So we're going to have to be resilient here. I think this group is another level advanced from that. They've been through a lot."

Taking down the Dodgers is a significant chapter in the Brewers' story. Milwaukee is now the first team in MLB playoff history to sweep a team that swept them the previous year. And against the team that has struck dread into opponents across baseball for the past two seasons, the Brewers showed that this iteration of their team is not easily shaken .

"I can't speak for anybody else, but for me, watching the way they carried themselves on the field after sweeping us last year was a little bit eye-opening," NLCS MVP Jake Bauers said after Game 4 on Thursday. "We won the NLDS against the Cubs [in 2025], and I think we kind of celebrated like that was something.

"Those guys swept us, they sent us home, and you would have thought it was a handshake line at a spring training game. That's something that I carried with me. That's something that I remembered. Yeah, it was a little bit of motivation to just say, we've got to keep going until there's not another game left to play."

That the Brewers defeated the back-to-back World Series champions really shouldn't come as a surprise. While a sweep might not have been on anyone's radar, this Brewers team has shown for most of the season that it's one of baseball's best. But the journey to end more than four decades of disappointments, failures and heartbreak didn't begin over the past two years.

Milwaukee's climb to the National League pennant has been slow and methodical over the past decade. In that time, the Brewers have become a model of consistency. They've become one of the best organizations in baseball as a result .

"There's a lot of people that picked them to be 82 wins, 83 wins, and I think we're at 110 and counting," Murphy said following the Brewers' NLCS sweep. "It just goes to show you the group that's in the room. They bought into each other. They bought into team."

The Brewers have reached the postseason in eight of the past nine seasons and have made three trips to the NLCS. They've averaged 94 wins over the past eight full seasons (excluding shortened 2020 season) and have been the postseason's No. 1 seed in back-to-back years. This trip to the Fall Classic has been a long time coming.

The first time the Dodgers faced the Brewers in the NLCS in 2018, the organization looked completely different. They were led by David Stearns, now the New York Mets' president of baseball operations, and manager Craig Counsell, now with the rival Chicago Cubs. After Stearns' departure in 2022 and Counsell's in 2023, there was some thought that Milwaukee's run of success might end.

History will show it was only a blip on the franchise's radar, as the partnership between Arnold and Murphy, both promoted in the wake of those departures, has helped take the organization to another level.

In 2026, the Brewers finished the season second in MLB in runs scored, but after they tied for 28th in homers, many wondered if their offensive success could continue in the postseason. Well, in these playoffs, Milwaukee leads all teams in homers, slugging percentage and OPS, along with average and on-base percentage, showing its offense is as good as any.

"You can't win this game by yourself," second baseman Brice Turang said. "You got to trust in your teammates to get it done. And if that's moving a guy over, then you move the guy over. And sometimes in trying to move them over, you drive a ball in the gap, and you end up scoring them. So you end up doing yourself a favor. So I think, when you play that way, good things happen."

The story of the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers is not yet finished, as they will host Games 1 and 2 of the Fall Classic next week in Milwaukee. But this team isn't a Cinderella story. The Brewers are a National League behemoth that has been building toward this success for quite some time.

Now four wins away from their ultimate goal with a roster that is one of the youngest in the sport, this might be just their beginning.

The Milwaukee Brewers were never just going to be defined by their accomplishments. When the smallest media market in MLB topples the two-time reigning champions to reach their first world Series in 44 years, the narrative will invariably transcend the action on the field. Pat Murphy's ballclub overcame a bottom-half payroll and swept the mighty Los Angeles Dodgers . This is not exactly a plucky underdog tale, however.

Nick Saban did not pull out a glass slipper or a slingshot when discussing Milwaukee's historic achievement. While he did express some surprise over the swift dispatching of LA, the all-time great college football head coach chose to underscore the winning team's greatness .

"The Brewers won more games than anybody," Saban said on Friday's episode of "The Pat McAfee Show." "I love it and they are great. They play good defense, they got team speed, they put the ball in play…. They just do a great job, and they hit home runs in this series. I really didn't think anybody could beat the Dodgers, but they swept them."

There is the temptation to slap a label on this franchise, whether it be "savvy" or "gritty" or "fundamentally sound." But perhaps the best word to sum up this squad is "elite." The Brew Crew did not use strictly small-ball and analytics to "beat the system."

Sure, they bunt a ton, steal bases and rely heavily on their bullpen, but this group can also adapt when necessary. Ohtani, now 32 years old, was placed on the injury list in early September to deal with biceps and knee concerns. articles.title: With many records set by the Brewers, this was one for the books. Literally.
articles.summary: Some of the records set in the NLCS underscore the David vs. Goliath storyline of the Brewers' championship.
articles.body:
Brewers vs Dodgers highlights, National League Championship Series Game 4

With a payroll about $195 million less than Los Angeles Dodgers, the Milwaukee Brewers now appear to hold the record for largest payroll deficit overcome in Major League Baseball post-season history.

Add in luxury tax penalties imposed on the Dodgers in 2026, and the disparity rises to about $278 million. The Dodgers' luxury tax penalties alone add up to more than the Brewers' entire payroll.

That information not only underscores the David vs. Goliath storyline of the Brewers National League championship, it also hints at how no game lends itself more to statistical comparisons than baseball.

Thanks to mlb.com, espn.com and some of our own number crunching, here are some more statistics coming out of the Brewers sweep of the Dodgers.

Over the four games, the Brewers had 128 at bats, 32 hits, a .250 batting average, and a .347 on-base percentage. Those are the exact same statistics as the Dodgers had when they won last year.

The Brewers are the first team in MLB history to sweep an opponent in the NLCS that swept them in the previous year's NLCS. It was the ultimate revenge sweep.

This was first sweep in an MLB postseason series between two teams with at least 100 wins during the regular season.

When the Brewers came back from 4-0 in game 4 to beat the Dodgers 6-4, Milwaukee completed the largest comeback to clinch a best-of-seven sweep in MLB history.

Milwaukee is the first team in MLB history to sweep in a best-of-seven postseason series despite trailing in every game. Beyond that, the Brewers are the first team in MLB history with six comeback wins over its first eight games of a postseason. They now have a 40-37 record, including playoffs, when their opponent scores the first run.

The Brewers are the first team in MLB history to have bullpen pitchers earn the win in all four games of a best-of-seven series sweep. All of the Brewers' wins this postseason have been credited to relief pitchers, which is unprecedented.

Brewers relievers threw five perfect innings to close out Game 2, the most of any team's bullpen in a postseason game.

The opportunity for more post-season records begins with the first game of the World Series on Friday, Oct. 23, at American Family Field.

articles.title: Two of MLB's smallest spenders will meet in the World Series for first time since 1991
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — When the Milwaukee defeated the mighty, monied Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night, they set up the first World Series between two of baseb...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — When the Milwaukee defeated the mighty, monied Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night, they set up the first World Series between two of baseball's smallest spenders in 35 years — just as team owners are arguing that clubs like the Brewers need a salary cap to compete consistently.

Milwaukee will face Cleveland or Tampa Bay in a best-of-seven series for the title beginning Oct. 23, ensuring two clubs in the bottom half of big league payrolls will play in the World Series for the first time since 1991. The Dodgers, New York Mets and New York Yankees will watch from home with payrolls this season that each cost more than the Brewers', Guardians' and Rays' rosters combined.

The low-budget World Series showdown will start six weeks before a likely management lockout, a work stoppage that threatens the 2027 season as owners and players battle over the sport's lack of a salary cap.

Speaking at the All-Star Game in July, baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred made his case for a cap while saying exceptions did not reflect parity.

"Our view of the world is that over a very long period of time there's a very strong relationship between who gets into the playoffs and who proceeds, notwithstanding the exceptions we've got," he said.

Milwaukee, which won the NL pennant with a four-game sweep of the Dodgers, had MLB's 19th-highest payroll as of Aug. 31, while Tampa Bay was 25th and Cleveland 30th. The last time both pennant winners were among the bottom 50% in player spending was when Minnesota (15th among 26 teams) beat Atlanta (19th) for the 1991 championship.

In terms of market size, Milwaukee ranks as MLB's 30th and smallest Designated Market Area, defined by Nielsen as non-overlapping geographic regions that group counties based on television viewing areas. Cleveland is 22nd and Tampa Bay 15th.

If the Guardians win the AL pennant, this would mark the first World Series involving two teams in the bottom half of MLB cities by DMA since St. Louis (24th) beat Detroit (18th) in 2006. No small-market team has won the World Series since Kansas City in 2015.

Three years after the Twins won that 1991 title, players went on strike as owners pushed for a salary cap, leading to the cancellation of the World Series. No such cap was added, and owners hadn't proposed one again until this summer.

Since the 1991 Twins, the only World Series winners with bottom-half payrolls have been the 2002 Anaheim Angels, 2003 Florida Marlins and 2017 Houston Astros.

"It's how the game is played in the moment dictates winning outcomes," agent Scott Boras said Friday. "There's no question that the probabilities of winning, success, are increased with greater talent, but we all know that talent has many variables as to how it performs at times."

MLB owners have proposed a salary cap with a floor, a system players say they will never accept. A lockout is likely to start Dec. 2.

Opening-day payrolls were topped by the Mets ($358.4 million), Dodgers ($323.3 million) and Yankees ($302.8 million). The Brewers were at $125.9 million, the Rays $90.5 million and the Guardians $75.5 million.

"Don't believe what you hear from the owner who's complaining: 'I don't have the resources to compete,'" players' association head Bruce Meyer said at the All-Star Game. "They all have the resources to compete. Our proposals include provisions that would give them more resources and reward the teams that actually do compete."

Manfred maintains spending big increases the odds of success.

"It defies human experience to ask a fan to think that the bottom end of that gap has the same opportunity to win as the top," he said. "There is no question that everybody in any sport is not going to win once every 30 or 32 years depending on how many teams you have, but the data in our sport is stark: Your opportunity to make the playoffs if you are a larger-market team is dramatically higher and your opportunity to proceed to the subsequent rounds, that advantage grows with each round."

articles.title: As Dodgers grapple with the end of a dynasty, questions abound for Shohei Ohtani, free agency and the coming labor fight
articles.summary: A stunningly comprehensive NLCS sweep by the Milwaukee Brewers casts onto the most expensive team ever assembled a foreign feeling: failure.
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, the unfamiliarity outshined the shock.

The defeated 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers, many of them back-to-back champs, hadn't been forced to face this uncomfortable silence in a while. A four-game drubbing courtesy of the Milwaukee Brewers in a stunningly comprehensive NLCS sweep cast onto the most expensive team ever assembled a very foreign feeling: failure.

Milwaukee, so often bounced early in the October melee, knows that discomfort and its soundtrack. That unsettling hush that comes with the humbling unmooring of a premature postseason exit. Hugs, daps, thank yous, low-volume answers, goodbyes, regrets. But here it was, here the Dodgers were, in the tricked-out home clubhouse grappling with the end of something.

On one side of the room, Shohei Ohtani stood in front of his locker before a massive semicircle of reporters and TV cameras. For the first time in his MLB career, he'd lost a postseason series. His signing with L.A. ahead of the 2024 season sparked this era of supercharged dominance. And for eight October series his Dodgers were untouchable. Usually, during this spot in the calendar, Ohtani is getting drenched in imitation champagne as Latin rap and joyous roars echo in the background.

The scene Thursday night was a drier, quieter experience.
