This seemingly indomitable baseball behemoth donned street clothes and a New Balance backward cap, small beads of sweat still pooling on his face, trying to explain what went wrong and where he goes from here.

"I haven't been able to really come to grips in terms of what I've learned overall this season," Ohtani said via interpreter Will Ireton. "I'm going to go back to the drawing board in terms of treatment, training program and see what I can come up with next season."

The postmortem on Los Angeles' crash-out can be as extensive as you choose to make it. But simply put, they were the inferior team. Slower, older, colder and less fearsome than the hard-charging Brewers . Baseball's most aged offense failed to slug and didn't perform with runners in scoring position. One of the most talented rotations ever assembled wasn't dominant enough to make up the difference.

All season, the Dodgers touted their experience as a calling card. Perhaps, if the series had been closer, that might have mattered. As it stands, it's less necessary to assign blame when so much went wrong.

"I think for me, it never feels good to lose, but when you get beat, you can handle it a little bit better," manager Dave Roberts said after his team's 6-4 loss in Game 4 .

The morning after, fans across the baseball universe are celebrating the Dodgers' downfall. They aren't the only ones. As Milwaukee's champagne celebration roared in the visiting clubhouse, Brewers coaches and executives were already receiving texts of appreciation and congratulations on slaying the mighty dragon.

But don't expect the upcoming small-market Fall Classic to remedy baseball's impending labor struggle. With the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1 , the league and the owners have been pushing hard for the adoption of a salary cap. Certainly, that argument becomes at least somewhat trickier to make with the half-billion-dollar boogeyman Dodgers on vacation, but the league won't suddenly change course after four games. The showdown over a cap was always going to be drawn-out and messy, no matter which team is the last one standing.

For the Dodgers organization, the uncertainty about baseball's future further complicates what was always going to be a critical offseason. One October exit won't kill off this juggernaut. Neither will a new economic landscape. The Dodgers remain advantageously positioned to compete for championships over the next decade and beyond. That's a testament to both their player-development prowess and their imposing spending power.

But the questions are already piling on Andrew Friedman's desk. Surely, the president of baseball operations is already considering the future and how this winter will shape the 2027 Dodgers.

No task is more important than figuring out what went wrong with Ohtani's season. For three months, the two-way star was, for the first time as a Dodger, doing full two-way stardom. Another MVP felt like an inevitability. Then his biceps started barking. A start on the mound was pushed back, then scratched, then so was another. Ohtani didn't throw a single in-game pitch after July 3.

His attempts to get back on the mound then appeared to compromise his offensive talents. He got ice-cold in late August into September. His physicality began to fray. His body wasn't right. Eventually, the Dodgers had no choice but to place him on the injured list. Only over the last two days of the Dodgers' postseason did Ohtani look anything like himself .

Communication with the four-time MVP has rarely been perfect. Some of that is the language barrier. Some of that is Ohtani's lone ranger approach. But now both sides need to evaluate why a diminished version of Ohtani was forced to play through pain. After the Game 4 loss, Ohtani told reporters that he intends to pitch next season. In what capacity remains to be seen. It might behoove the Dodgers to slow-play his recovery timeline to ensure he's available when they need him most — in the postseason.

There are a mountain of transactional questions as well. Tarik Skubal, added in a deadline blockbuster, is now a free agent. Will the Dodgers flex their muscles to re-sign him? Or do they want to give younger arms such as Roki Sasaki, Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski some rotation runway? What about upper-level pitching prospects such as Christian Zazueta, Zach Root, Adam Serwinowski and Jackson Ferris? Could they let Skubal walk in favor of a different free-agent starter? Freddy Peralta has looked pretty good recently.

Positionally, though, is where Los Angeles' bigger roster-construction conversations will take place. They got mollywhopped by Milwaukee in part because the Dodgers' offense looked unathletic and elderly. Friedman has expressed a desire to inject more youth into the group, but that's easier said than done. A number of spots feel set in stone: Ohtani at DH, Will Smith at catcher, Freddie Freeman at first, Mookie Betts at short, Kyle Tucker in right field, Andy Pages in center.

Max Muncy (3B) and Teoscar Hernández (LF) are older players expected to reach free agency after 2027. A trade of either could be a way to reshuffle the deck, with Hernández the likelier to go. Tommy Edman had a second straight mediocre, injury-marred campaign, but he has four seasons left on his contract. Might the Dodgers seek a suitor for the switch-hitting utilityman?

Even after harvesting the farm for the Skubal trade, Los Angeles has one of the most stocked systems in the sport. Most of their prospect juice is concentrated in the outfield. Five Dodgers outfield prospects at Double-A or above — Josue De Paula, Eduardo Quintero, Mike Sirota, Charles Davalan and James Tibbs III — could find themselves on offseason top-100 lists. De Paula, who impressed in a late-season cup of coffee, Quintero and Sirota are currently ranked fourth, 15th and 17th, respectively, by MLB Pipeline.

Unfortunately for the Dodgers, you can play only three outfielders at a time. In their existing outfield, they already have the highest-paid player in the sport (Tucker) and the starting center fielder in the 2026 All-Star Game (Pages). With just one spot remaining, it'll be fascinating to see how Friedman makes use of his farm system.

For the players, none of these contingencies or scenarios will offer any short-term solace. They aimed for a three-peat and missed. That sting will take time to subside, even if the 2027 Dodgers project to be a similarly formidable force.

"We fell short, you know?" utilityman Kiké Hernández lamented postgame. "We had a good run, but here we are."

articles.title: Rays vs. Guardians ALCS Game 4 Postponed Due to Inclement Weather, Photos & Videos of Rain, Puddles
articles.summary: Rainy conditions at Progressive Field has caused Game 4 of the ALCS to be postponed.
articles.body:
Rainy conditions at Progressive Field has caused Game 4 of the ALCS to be postponed.

The Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays will instead play on Saturday at 8 p.m. to continue the series.

The game was initially in a delay for about an hour before officials decide to make the decision to postpone.

The heavy rain had resulted in puddles forming on the warning track.

Weather has influenced the series since it shifted to Cleveland, as Thursday's Game 3 was moved up from 6 p.m. ET to 1 p.m. ET in order to avoid rain.

Before the start time of Game 4 was changed, there were conversations held regarding a potential update.

Nick Camino of WKYC-TV 3 reported Friday that the Guardians and Rays had a meeting with MLB at 6 p.m. ET to discuss the weather situation and the possibility of moving the beginning of the contest.

Cleveland holds a 2-1 series lead over Tampa Bay, securing a 7-3 victory in Game 1 before wrapping up a 3-2 win in Game 3. The Rays won Game 2 by the final score of 3-1.

The Guardians are looking to move one step closer to capturing the AL pennant and contending for the first World Series title since 1948, while the Rays are attempting to continue their journey to win the Fall Classic for the first time in franchise history.

articles.title: Orioles owner David Rubenstein says quiet part out loud before lockout: His MLB peers are making a ton of money
articles.summary: The Orioles owner had some interesting things to say about the league's finances.
articles.body:
All indications are that we are headed toward an MLB lockout once the 2026 season is over. If that's the case, Baltimore Orioles owner David Rubenstein said the exact opposite of what owners are supposed to say on Thursday.

Speaking with a group of other local team owners at the Economic Club of Washington, D.C., Rubenstein was discussing the unexpected challenges of owning an MLB team when he threw in a little nugget about his thought process in buying the Orioles in the first place.

"A lot of my friends were buying teams, and I realized they're making money. They're making more money than I'm making in private equity," he said. "I thought I should look at it as a financial thing, but ultimately, I bought the Orioles for a philanthropic purpose."

Rubenstein purchased a majority stake in the Orioles from the Angelos family in 2024, at a valuation of $1.725 billion.

It feels obvious to say that MLB owners are making a ton of money, with the income apparently surpassing even what Rubenstein makes from The Carlyle Group private equity firm he co-founded ( which drove his estimated net worth above $4 billion ). Billionaires rarely buy something if they aren't going to make money from it.

However, that's not the image the owners will be projecting once the likely lockout begins. They want a salary cap, so we are about to hear a lot about how the league's finances are unsustainable without a salary cap and how small-market teams such as Rubenstein's Orioles need a salary cap to compete with large-market teams such as the Los Angeles Dodgers ( pay no attention to what happened to that team on Thursday ).

Rubenstein himself has called for a salary cap multiple times. Unless his MLB friends are some combination of Mark Walter (Dodgers), Steve Cohen (New York Mets), John Henry (Boston Red Sox) and the Steinbrenner family (New York Yankees), what he just said undercuts the financial necessity of a cap.

Rubenstein did claim that his peers care about winning more than making money:

"Lots of people want to be owners and lots of people don't realize how hard it is to be an owner. I keep telling people, it's not as easy as I thought," he said. "The owners care more about winning than making money. They're not against making money. Of course, they don't want to lose money. The obsession with winning and beating your competitors is really what drives these people who own these teams. There's nothing as satisfying as winning a championship."

"Lots of people want to be owners and lots of people don't realize how hard it is to be an owner. I keep telling people, it's not as easy as I thought," he said.

"The owners care more about winning than making money. They're not against making money. Of course, they don't want to lose money. The obsession with winning and beating your competitors is really what drives these people who own these teams. There's nothing as satisfying as winning a championship."

Of course, this only matters if public opinion matters in a labor negotiation. MLB has acted as if that's the case, using its main social media accounts to publicly negotiate with the MLB Players Association. But ultimately, it will be representatives of the owners and players in the negotiating room and no one else.

Rubenstein's Orioles tenure has so far not been as successful as hoped, given that he took over the team in the aftermath of a 101-win season with a promise to spend more than his predecessors. The 2024 Orioles were among baseball's more disappointing teams, falling to 91 wins and a wild-card sweep, and the team failed to break .500 in both 2025 and 2026.

That all adds up to a pivotal offseason in Baltimore, even beyond the CBA negotiations.

articles.title: Guardians-Rays MLB playoff game start delayed by rain
articles.summary: The start of the Cleveland Guardians' home playoff game against the Tampa Bay Rays was delayed after rain pounded Cleveland on Friday, but officials still ho...
articles.body:
The start of the Cleveland Guardians' home playoff game against the Tampa Bay Rays was delayed after rain pounded Cleveland on Friday, but officials still hoped to get the game underway.

The Guardians held a 2-1 lead in the best-of-seven American League Championship Series going into Friday's game four.

They are also scheduled to host game five on Saturday, with the teams due to travel to Florida on Sunday for games six and seven if necessary.

Less than an hour before the scheduled first pitch at 8:08 pm (00:08 GMT) Major League Baseball said in a statement that the game would "begin in a delay".

"We will provide updates regarding the preparation of the field and any other potential adjustments as they become available."

Grounds crew briefly removed the protective tarp covering the infield and began working to clear standing water on the warning track shortly before the original scheduled start time.

The forecast called for intermittent showers and chilly temperatures for much of the night.

The Rays are chasing their first World Series title, having come up short in the Fall Classic in 2008 and 2020.

Cleveland are out to end the longest active title drought in MLB, having last won it all in 1948. Cleveland have been to the World Series four times since then and come up empty, most recently in 2016.

The winners of the series will take on the Milwaukee Brewers in the World Series starting on October 23.

The Brewers swept the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers 4-0 in the National League Championship Series.
